#6173. Southwest Premier Business Card Review: Is The $149 Annual Fee Worth It?

The Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card is the more basic of the two Southwest business cards. This card has a $149 annual fee, and gets you a handful of valuable benefits when you fly Southwest, including complimentary upgrades to Preferred seating within 48 hours of departure and a free checked bag, among other things.

If you fly Southwest at least a few times a year and you qualify for a small business credit card, the Southwest Premier Business Card is worth considering. It’s worth an extra close look right now, because now is your last chance to earn a Southwest credit card welcome bonus that counts toward the airline’s valuable Companion Pass benefit. I’ll get into all that and more below in my comprehensive Southwest Premier Business Card review.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card

Before getting into the Southwest Premier Business Card in detail, let’s take a broader look at the card’s main features:

I also put together my pros and cons for the Southwest Premier Business Card:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is Southwest’s entry-level business credit card. Let’s take a look at the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and annual fee, given that these are factors that many people consider when applying for a card.

The Southwest Premier Business Card currently has a welcome bonus where you can earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 within the first three months.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each, as that’s roughly the rate at which you can redeem points toward flights. So by my valuation, 60,000 Rapid Rewards points are worth ~$720.

While this is a decent welcome offer, let me note that we’ve seen bigger limited time welcome offers in the past. So if you’re primarily after the best welcome offer, it could make sense to wait to apply.

The welcome bonus on the Southwest Premier Business Card isn’t available to those who currently have this card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible for this card (including the welcome bonus) if you have the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more), or any personal Southwest credit card.

Also remember Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, apply. With the 5/24 rule, you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the last 24 months. However, business credit cards aren’t always included on your credit report, so they often don’t count toward 5/24.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a $149 annual fee. There’s no cost to add additional users to the card. You can set individual spending limits for additional cards, and you can earn points on their spending.

The Southwest Premier Business Card doesn’t charge any foreign transaction fees, so you can use it abroad without worrying about racking up extra charges.

Obviously the rewards structure is an important factor to consider when applying for a credit card. So how does the Southwest Premier Business Card do on that front? In addition to offering bonus points in select spending categories, the card also offers the ability to earn status through spending, so let’s cover those details.

As far as the rewards structure goes, the Southwest Premier Business Card offers:

While these are some good bonus categories, I wouldn’t consider this to be an industry-leading rewards structure — there are better cards for airfare spending, and better cards for everyday spending.

Based on my valuation of Southwest points at 1.2 cents each, using the Southwest Premier Business Card to book Southwest flights gets you a 3.6% return on spending, while the 2x and 1x categories get you 2.4% and 1.2% returns on spending, respectively.

Spending on the Southwest Premier Business Card can count toward A-List elite status. Specifically, through the end of 2026 you can earn 2,000 Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward A-List for every $5,000 you spend on the card. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on the card will earn one TQP.

A-List status ordinarily requires 35,000 TQPs per year, and offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number.

However, Southwest has announced some big changes to its loyalty program, including new status level names and the introduction of a third tier called Platinum. Starting in 2027, A-List status will become Silver status. Earning it will require 35,000 TQPs (unchanged) or 25 qualifying flights (up from 20 today).

Personally I probably wouldn’t spend that much money on a credit card to earn A-List status, but for some people this could prove to be worthwhile, especially if you’re close to earning A-List status otherwise.

One of the very best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. With Southwest Companion Pass, you can have someone travel with you for the entire year (whether on a cash ticket or award ticket), and just pay taxes and fees for them. This is such an incredible deal, and basically doubles the value you can get from flying Southwest. The pass is valid for the rest of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the following full year, so the earlier in the year you earn it, the more it’s worth.

Historically, you’ve been able to get the Companion Pass by earning 135,000 Rapid Rewards points in a calendar year — and Southwest credit card welcome bonuses counted toward this, along with referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending on the card, and more. Starting January 1, 2027, though, this will no longer be the case.

Southwest is updating its elite status program to have three tiers, the highest of which is called Platinum and gets you unlimited Companion Pass trips. At that time, credit card welcome bonuses and all the other points earning mentioned above will no longer count toward qualifying for the Companion Pass (or any level of status).

To earn Platinum, and therefore the Companion Pass, you’ll instead need to earn 140,000 TQPs or take 100 qualifying flights. This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Premier Business Card; it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that points from the current welcome bonus offer do count toward Companion Pass qualification for the rest of 2026 and through 2027, per Chase’s offer details, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity is closed.

I have an entire post on how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work and how to get the most value out of your points here.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, with Basic awards usually offering the highest redemption value.

In my experience, the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. Southwest also flies to Hawaii, which can be a good use of points, but I’ve found that the redemption value is often a bit lower on these in-demand routes. And of course, if you have the Companion Pass your points become twice as valuable because a friend can travel for free minus taxes and fees.

There are no change or cancellation fees on Southwest award bookings, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d want to cancel and rebook rather than change your existing itinerary.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a solid welcome bonus that’s especially valuable now that it’s your last chance to earn it and have it count toward the Companion Pass, but that’s not the only reason to consider this card. There are also several ongoing perks that can make your experience flying Southwest a little more comfortable.

One major ongoing perk of the Southwest Premier Business Card is that you earn 6,000 Rapid Rewards bonus points on your account anniversary every year. As mentioned above, I value Rapid Rewards points at around 1.2 cents each, so to me, that’s like $72 worth of value annually.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a free first checked bag for you and up to eight additional passengers on your same reservation.

If you usually check bags on Southwest — especially if you don’t have Southwest status, which gets you a free first checked bag — this benefit alone can help you recoup the annual fee. For non-elite Southwest travelers, a checked bag costs $45 one-way, so you could save $90 on a roundtrip flight. With two roundtrip flights with checked bags in a year, that already cancels out the $149 annual fee.

As a Southwest Premier Business cardholder, you can select a Preferred or Standard seat within 48 hours prior to departure, if they’re available. This benefit also extends to eight travelers on your same reservation. The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight.

The Southwest Premier Business Card also gets you a 15% promo code each year on your account anniversary. You can use this to score a 15% discount on a Southwest flight, excluding Basic fares. This perk is another nice way the card can save you money when flying Southwest, especially if you book cash tickets in addition to award flights at least once a year.

Southwest Premier Business cardholders can board with Group 5, or earlier if they have status or a fare that entitles them to a higher boarding group. This perk extends to eight additional travelers on the same reservation.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers 25% savings on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases on Southwest. Just charge your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for 25% of the purchase total, which should appear within two billing cycles.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a great welcome bonus, and the $149 annual fee can be largely offset by the 6,000 anniversary bonus points and other benefits. The welcome bonus can also go a long way toward earning the Companion Pass, which is all the more reason to get the card now before this opportunity ends.

That said, I don’t necessarily think the Southwest Premier Business Card is a great pick for everyone. If you’re not loyal to Southwest or you split flying across multiple airlines, it’s probably not the best card for you. And if you want flexible points that you can redeem with a variety of airlines and hotels, it could also be best to skip this card.

First, let me compare it to the more premium Southwest Performance Business Card, then I’ll share the points currency I recommend earning instead if you’re mainly concerned with booking award flights on Southwest, not extra perks with the airline.

The Southwest Performance Business Card (learn more) is the more premium sibling of the Southwest Premier Business Card. Overall it comes with more benefits — and in some cases enhanced versions of the same perks on the Southwest Premier Business Card.

Here’s a quick overview of how the Southwest business credit cards compare:

The extra 3,000 anniversary points are worth $36 by my valuation, so you’d need roughly $9,500 in Southwest spending for the extra point per dollar to cover the rest of the $150 fee difference, before counting the seating and Global Entry perks.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and you want as many perks and points as possible, the Southwest Performance Business Card could be worth the higher annual fee.

If your goal is to earn Southwest Rapid Rewards points, but you don’t actually plan on earning the Companion Pass or Southwest status, there’s a much faster way to earn those points.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. You can earn points at a much faster rate with the following business cards:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is a good entry-level Southwest Airlines business credit card with a nice welcome bonus. The current bonus can earn you a lot of travel on Southwest, and can even help you earn Companion Pass — but only if you earn the bonus under the current offer, before the 2027 program changes take effect.

This card is definitely worth considering, though the only other consideration is that I think it could be worth paying the premium for the Southwest Performance Business Card, which has better ongoing perks. And earning Ultimate Rewards points with a Chase credit card could also make more sense unless you really value the Southwest-specific benefits.

Which Southwest business credit card do you prefer?

#6170. Hyatt Dining & Spa Awards: Are They Worth Redeeming Points For?

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night award redemptions, there are some lesser known ways to redeem Hyatt points. One of those is the ability to use points for Dining & Spa awards, which can be a surprisingly good deal.

This doesn’t get a lot of attention, and it’s particularly useful if you want to minimize your out-of-pocket when staying at a Hyatt property, while still indulging in on-property experiences.

Most people don’t realize that you can redeem World of Hyatt points toward the cost of on-property dining and spa experiences, and the value proposition can be surprisingly good. Specifically, you can redeem a certain number of points for a certain amount of credit to use toward on-property spending, even if you’re not staying at a Hyatt property. Let’s take a closer look at how this works.

Below is a chart showing the various redemption opportunities available with Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards, along with how much value you can potentially get per point:

As you can see, you can redeem anywhere from 1,000 points for a $10 credit, to 65,000 points for a $1,000 credit. The value per point ranges anywhere from 1.0 cents per point, to 1.54 cents per point.

1.54 cents per World of Hyatt point sounds like a solid deal. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, World of Hyatt points are worth 1.4 cents each, so this actually offers solid value, at least on the surface. Is there a catch, though?

The exact redemptions that are allowed vary by hotel, but generally you can expect that these awards can be used for food and beverage purchases, spa and salon services, and spa and salon retail items.

On top of that, when charged to a member’s guest room, the following charges may be eligible:

laundry, dry cleaning, telephone charges, pay-per-view movies, parking, gift/retail shop, service charges, taxes (not including room taxes) and gratuities

Meanwhile the following charges are expressly prohibited from being eligible:

room rates, room taxes, alcoholic beverages (in certain jurisdictions), catering or banquet charges, and casino charges

If you’re staying at a Hyatt then you should be able to redeem these awards for cumulative charges over the course of your stay. However, I’d recommend confirming this with the front desk at check-in, including which outlets would be eligible for these redemptions, since individual hotels could have different policies.

Not all Hyatt hotels participate in this program. Miraval, Unscripted by Hyatt, Hyatt Select, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Vacation Club properties, Hyatt Vivid, Bahia Principe, Impression by Secrets, Secrets, Dreams, Breathless, Zoëtry, Alua, Sunscape, and other Legacy AMR Collection resorts, as well as some Dream properties, do not participate. Furthermore, redemption of these certificates is limited to registered guests at Hyatt Zilara, Hyatt Ziva, and Hyatt Studios properties.

To be positive, you can search participating properties at this page.

You don’t need to redeem for these certificates in advance, but rather the World of Hyatt member should just inform the Hyatt employee at the eligible outlet that they’d like to redeem points toward their purchase at the outset. You’ll need to have your membership information, and should then be asked how many points you want to redeem.

If you’re a registered guest at a hotel then you can apply one of these at check-out toward multiple purchases over the course of a stay. If you’re not a registered guest then you’ll have to settle your folio at the particular outlet you’re at.

There are a few other things to potentially be aware of:

On the surface, being able to redeem World of Hyatt points for up to ~1.54 cents toward the cost of a purchase is a solid deal. Is it exceptional? No. But as a way of essentially “cashing out” your points to offset cash costs I think it’s very good.

I do think it’s important to create a more realistic valuation of these redemptions, though. When you redeem these awards you’re forgoing the opportunity to earn points on these purchases:

As a Globalist member I earn 10.5x points per dollar spent, which I value at a return of ~15% (1.4 cents per point). That’s an opportunity cost that’s worth factoring in, so in reality, I’d adjust the maximum value from 1.54 cents to ~1.3 cents.

Personally, this isn’t how I’d redeem my World of Hyatt points, though I do think many people could find this to be worthwhile for a splurge:

World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, allowing members to redeem points for dining and spa experiences at most Hyatt properties. This has the potential to be a solid deal, as getting 1.54 cents per Hyatt point toward the cost of a purchase is a good redemption. However, do factor in the points you’re forgoing, which brings down the redemption value a bit.

While I wouldn’t say this is the best way to redeem Hyatt points, this could be worth it to lower how much cash you’ll pay for a Hyatt stay, especially at a secluded resort where you’re likely to spend most time on-property.

What do you make of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards? Could you see yourself redeeming points for them?

#6168. How Emirates Safeguards Its Longest Airbus A380 Route With A Little-Known Fallback

Operating the world's longest Airbus A380 route is an achievement that demands far more than simply assigning the aircraft with the greatest passenger capacity. Every flight between Dubai International Airport (DXB) and Auckland Airport (AKL) requires careful planning, significant fuel reserves, favorable weather conditions, and enough operational flexibility to cope with changing winds across thousands of miles of ocean and remote airspace.

While the nonstop service often attracts attention because of its remarkable duration, the supporting strategy behind it is equally noteworthy. Since launching the route in 2016, Emirates has quietly maintained an alternative network that allows passengers to reach New Zealand even when the airline adjusts nonstop operations.

Rather than relying exclusively on a single ultra-long-haul flight, the Dubai-based carrier has preserved one-stop connections through Australia, creating a practical fallback that strengthens resilience while giving planners greater freedom to respond to operational challenges and changing market demand.

The nonstop route between DXB and AKL has occupied a unique position within Emirates' network since its introduction in March 2016. Covering approximately 8,800 miles (14,162 km), the flight represents the airline's longest scheduled A380 operation and remains among the longest commercial flights operated anywhere in the world.

Although the eastbound journey from Auckland to Dubai is lengthy in its own right, the westbound flight usually presents the greater challenge because of prevailing winds across the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia. Under favorable conditions, the journey can be completed in a little over 17 hours, but strong headwinds have regularly extended block times to around 17 hours and 25 minutes.

This makes every departure a carefully planned balancing act involving payload, fuel, weather forecasts, and air traffic considerations. These operational realities mean that dispatchers cannot simply schedule the same aircraft performance every day throughout the year. Seasonal wind patterns influence fuel requirements, while unexpected weather systems may require revised routings that add additional flying time.

Even relatively small changes become significant on flights lasting well over 17 hours, where every additional minute increases fuel consumption and operational complexity. Despite these challenges, Emirates has continued to assign the A380 exclusively to the route.

This highlights the carrier's confidence in the aircraft's capabilities. The double-decker provides substantial passenger capacity across premium and economy cabins while also offering the range needed for one of commercial aviation's most demanding missions.

While the nonstop route receives the majority of public attention, Emirates has never depended on it as the sole means of serving Auckland. Instead, the airline has continued operating extensive services into Australia's largest cities, allowing passengers to connect onward to New Zealand whenever necessary.

Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) has traditionally played the most prominent role within this strategy thanks to its extensive schedule from Dubai and its large volume of connecting passengers. Emirates also maintains significant operations into Melbourne Airport (MEL) and Brisbane Airport (BNE), creating multiple pathways for travelers heading toward Auckland without requiring the airline to depend entirely on the nonstop service.

This approach gives Emirates an established backup within its broader network rather than requiring special contingency planning whenever operational conditions become less favorable. If schedules change or nonstop frequencies are reduced, passengers can still travel between Dubai and Auckland through Australian gateways using connections that have long been integrated into the airline's system.

The arrangement also benefits customers originating outside Dubai, as Emirates carries passengers from across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia through its Dubai hub before distributing them across its long-haul network. Having several onward routing options increases flexibility throughout the reservation system and helps minimize disruption when demand patterns shift.

Flights lasting more than 17 hours leave little room for operational uncertainty. Airline planners must consider aircraft performance, passenger loads, cargo demand, weather forecasts, alternate airports, and regulatory fuel requirements before every departure. Unlike shorter international routes, adjustments cannot easily be absorbed once the aircraft is airborne because diversion options remain limited across large stretches of ocean.

Headwinds represent one of the most important variables affecting Dubai-Auckland operations, and strong winds opposing the aircraft increase fuel burn and can reduce operational margins, particularly on the westbound sector. As a result, planners continuously evaluate expected atmospheric conditions before finalizing payload and fuel calculations.

Maintaining one-stop alternatives through Australia provides an additional layer of flexibility within this process, as rather than insisting that every passenger travel nonstop regardless of operating conditions, Emirates can adapt schedules according to seasonal requirements while continuing to offer reliable service between Dubai and New Zealand.

The strategy also supports efficient fleet utilization. A380 examples represent valuable assets that must be allocated carefully across the airline's global network. Having multiple routing options allows Emirates to deploy aircraft where demand is strongest while preserving connectivity even when operational priorities evolve during different times of the year.

Four out of the seven routes use the Boeing 787.

Although the Australian connection strategy remains in place, passenger demand has increasingly favored the nonstop option. As international travel continued to recover and long-haul markets strengthened, Emirates gradually expanded nonstop operations between Dubai and Auckland.

A significant milestone arrived earlier this year, when the airline increased the route to daily A380 service. The schedule expansion reflected confidence in sustained demand while demonstrating that the economics of operating one of the world's longest flights remained attractive despite its considerable operating costs.

Even with daily nonstop flights, however, the underlying network philosophy has not changed. The Australian gateways continue serving an important role by providing additional capacity, supporting passengers whose itineraries involve Australian destinations, and preserving operational resilience whenever circumstances require adjustments. Rather than replacing the connecting model, the expanded non-stop schedule complements it.

Together, both options create a network that can accommodate different passenger preferences while allowing Emirates to respond to changes in demand without sacrificing connectivity across the region. The result is a system that balances efficiency with redundancy, ensuring that one of the airline's most ambitious routes remains supported by a broader operational framework rather than existing in isolation.

Many airlines have reduced or retired A380 fleets over the past decade, yet Emirates has remained firmly committed to the type as the flagship of its long-haul operation. No carrier operates more A380s, and the aircraft continues serving numerous high-demand destinations throughout Europe, Asia, Australia, and North America.

The Dubai-Auckland route showcases many of the aircraft's strengths. Its combination of long range and high seating capacity allows Emirates to transport hundreds of passengers on a single flight while offering premium products that include onboard lounges and shower spas for first-class travelers.

Operating such a large aircraft on an ultra-long-haul route also improves efficiency when passenger demand supports high load factors. Instead of scheduling multiple smaller aircraft, Emirates can concentrate capacity into a single daily departure while maintaining a consistent onboard product across the route. The airline's continuing investment in cabin refurbishment programs further reinforces the importance of the A380 within its future plans.

Updated interiors, refreshed premium cabins, and modernized economy seating help ensure that the aircraft remains competitive despite its age, particularly on flights where passenger comfort becomes increasingly important after more than 17 hours in the air. As detailed in the table above, Emirates currently has a total of 116 Airbus A380s in its fleet, according to ch-aviation.

Why the Airbus A350-1000’s range, efficiency, and comfort can make it the ideal aircraft for Emirates’ ultra-long-haul global network.

From a passenger perspective, the non-stop Dubai-Auckland service appears to be a single record-setting flight linking two distant cities. Behind the scenes, however, it functions as one component within a much larger network built around flexibility, redundancy, and efficient aircraft utilization.

The continued availability of Australian connections demonstrates that successful ultra-long-haul operations depend as much on network planning as aircraft performance. By maintaining multiple routing options through Sydney, Melbourne, and Brisbane, Emirates reduces dependence on any single schedule while preserving service continuity across the broader region.

This philosophy has allowed the airline to adjust non-stop frequencies over time without abandoning the market or compromising connectivity. Whether operating fewer non-stop flights during certain periods or increasing the service to daily A380 departures when demand supports expansion, Emirates retains an established fallback that has been part of its strategy since the route first launched in 2016.

Rather than viewing the Australian services as competitors to the non-stop flight, Emirates has positioned them as complementary components of a broader network. That combination enables the airline to continue operating one of commercial aviation's most demanding Airbus A380 routes while maintaining the operational resilience needed for flights that regularly spend well over 17 hours in the air.

#6167. Baby Moose Wandered Up To Alaska Airlines Check-In Entrance — As One Man Shooes It Away

A baby moose trotted past passengers unloading their bags curbside at Anchorage airport, then stopped near the Alaska Airlines check-in doors. A man simply walked toward it, waved an arm, shooed it away getting it to turn around. The man sharing the video, describes the animal as trying to board an Alaska Airlines flight. If only! It walks past cars and travelers before it pausing near the terminal entrance – door 1 for Air Canada, Alaska Airlines and American. The animal passes close to an open SUV hatch as passengers handle their bags. Another traveler is standing outside the terminal with suitcases when the moose stops nearby. A man approaches from the roadway and the calf heads back along the sidewalk. There’s a potentially sad explanation for why it’s alone. A commenter who says he’s the one that shooed it away reports airport employees told him the calf’s mother had been hit and killed by a vehicle a few days earlier. Anchorage airport regularly reminds travelers about moose around its roads and parking areas. I’ve covered an Alaska Airlines flight delayed by a seal on the runway, polar bears on an Alaska airport taxiway, and a raccoon helping itself to candy at a Philadelphia airport shop. The raccoon at least knew what it wanted. #6165. 59-Room Andaz Turks & Caicos At Grace Bay Opening April 2027, Now Bookable

The much delayed Andaz Turks & Caicos is getting closer to opening. The hotel has now moved forward the date as of which it’s accepting reservations, and we’ve also learned more details about the on-property amenities. Let’s cover all the details, as we’re potentially under five months from the opening…

The Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. This will mark Hyatt’s first hotel in Turks & Caicos, and the first Andaz property in the Caribbean. For that matter, it’s one of the only Andaz properties that’s currently in the pipeline outside of Asia, as the brand has really lost steam.

The 5.5-acre resort will offer four restaurants and bars, three outdoor pools, a spa, a kids club, a fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, and more. The Andaz will be comprised of 59 rooms and 73 branded residences, so at least the hotel portion of the property will be boutique. It’ll be located directly on Grace Bay, known for offering one of the most beautiful stretches of beach in the Caribbean.

As far as the culinary concepts go, the Andaz Turks & Caicos will feature the following:

Runa Spa & Wellness, the spa at the Andaz, will be around 7,000 square feet. It will have five treatment rooms, along with a sauna, cold plunge, relaxation area, and more.

The opening of this resort has been majorly delayed. It was initially announced in 2018 with a 2021 opening, but the timeline slipped by six years, presumably due to a combination of the pandemic, plus… well, how hotel construction projects often work out. Hopefully there are no additional delays beyond the current planned spring 2027 opening.

With the Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay bookable, what are rates like? For those redeeming points, this is a Category 8 World of Hyatt property, meaning a free night redemption in a standard room costs 35,000-75,000 points per night.

World of Hyatt’s new award chart sure makes top end redemptions expensive, unfortunately! As of now the hotel is primarily bookable between April and November of 2027, so this doesn’t really cover peak season. For most dates, I currently see rates of either 35,000 points, 45,000 points, or 55,000 points per night. So value here is highly dependent on which of those rates you can find.

When it comes to cash rates, those currently start at around $900-1,300 per night, and that depends on when you’re staying. That’s inclusive of the service charge, but exclusive of the taxes.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, and a hotel credit.

I suppose good options on Grace Bay are limited, and this hotel is boutique. But at these rates, they better offer something significantly better than the typical Andaz experience, in my opinion.

Turks & Caicos is absolutely beautiful, and it’s an easy getaway from the United States, given how close it is to Florida. Historically, the country hasn’t had that many points hotels, though that’s slowly starting to change.

Several years back, we saw the opening of the Ritz-Carlton Turks & Caicos. It has an amazing location on Grace Bay and the grounds of the property are beautiful, but it otherwise doesn’t feel very luxurious, and lacks personality.

So it’ll be nice to have another points property, and I look forward to learning more about the Andaz. Maybe I’m overly optimistic, but I think the Andaz might just end up offering a better experience than the Ritz-Carlton, at least based on the design renderings, and also the more boutique scale of the property. Andaz really is quite an inconsistent brand.

I of course should acknowledge that many people are understandably frustrated by the way that Grace Bay has developed over the years, given all the huge concrete towers that have taken shape along the beach. It has definitely lost its charm a bit, though the beach is still gorgeous.

Even beyond Grace Bay, we’re seeing some other great new options in Turks & Caicos. In 2025, we saw the opening of Salterra Turks & Caicos, a Marriott Luxury Collection property. This is great for those who want a bit more secluded of a trip, since South Caicos Island is a bit less crowded than the area around Providenciales. This is also where Sailrock Resort is located, which is an independent hotel affiliated with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH).

There’s also a Waldorf Astoria Turks & Caicos planned for a 2028 opening, located on Dellis Cay, a nearby island that’s not as developed, which can be reached by a 25-minute boat transfer from Providenciales. That should also be a great option, especially with how the Waldorf Astoria portfolio is developing. However, don’t count on that timeline sticking either.

The Andaz Turks & Caicos is accepting reservations for stays as of April 2027, and it will be located on the famous Grace Bay. The property will have just 59 hotel rooms, in addition to residences, so I like how it’s on a smaller scale than some other properties.

This should be a very nice addition to the Caribbean points hotel market. Hopefully we don’t see any additional delays with the opening…

What do you make of the upcoming Andaz Turks & Caicos?

#6163. JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!

For whatever reason, JetBlue tends to be the industry leader when it comes to raising checked bag fees, and competitors tend to follow. Earlier this year, JetBlue was the first major US carrier to raise checked bag fees, and now the airline is raising checked bag fees again…

Effective immediately (for tickets purchased as of November 3, 2026), JetBlue has increased checked bag fees. JetBlue has a rather complicated fee structure for checked bags, with both off-peak and peak pricing, plus different pricing based on whether you pay for the bag 24 hours or more in advance.

Below is a chart with JetBlue’s new checked bag fees.

As you can see, an off-peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $50-60 (depending on whether you pay in advance), while a peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $55-70 (depending on whether you pay in advance). For context, below are the dates that are considered peak for the purposes of bag fees.

It goes without saying that paying $50-70 for a first checked bag is a pretty substantial cost, especially when you consider how little checked bags used to cost. On a one-way, you’re looking at $100-140. For a family of four, you’d be looking at $400-560.

When JetBlue raised checked bag fees earlier this year, the airline released a statement claiming it was increasing checked bag fees to be “more competitive,” and that “while we recognize that fee increases are never ideal, we take careful consideration to ensure these changes are implemented only when necessary.” I imagine this time around, the logic is much of the same.

The simple reality is that oil prices are way up. Airlines have actually done a solid job of being able to make fare increases stick. But that’s not enough to fully offset the increase in the cost of jet fuel.

JetBlue is in a rough financial spot, and it hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic. The airline is hoping to turn an operating profit in 2027, though that strikes me as being particularly optimistic. So the logic for raising checked bags is threefold:

JetBlue has just increased checked bag fees once again, and you’ll now pay $50-70 for a first checked bag on a domestic flight. This is JetBlue’s second price increase on checked bags so far this year. When airlines are trying to increase revenue, checked bag fees are often low hanging fruit.

When competitors match, it also becomes something that’s unavoidable for consumers, other than getting a credit card… which also has upside for the airline! I’d be shocked if other airlines don’t match this move from JetBlue.

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

Premium cards are not just about travel — they’re continuing to add lifestyle value you can use at home. The American Express Platinum Card® offers up to $75 per quarter (up to $300 per calendar year) in Lululemon statement credits.*

Whether you're looking for casual attire, travel essentials or workout gear, here are seven items we recommend buying with your quarterly $75 Lululemon statement credit.

*Enrollment is required, and outlets are excluded. Only applies to purchases at U.S. stores and online.

Although the Amex Platinum's $895 annual fee (see ) may seem very high, perks like the quarterly up to $75 Lululemon statement credit (up to $300 each calendar year) help offset the cost.

The up to $75 quarterly statement credit is valid for eligible purchases made at U.S. Lululemon stores (excluding outlets) and on lululemon.com (after enrollment).

Many TPGers are big fans of Lululemon and find its clothing to be an excellent choice for travel-day outfits. It's also comfortable for city travel and lightweight for exercise.

Related: How to maximize benefits with the Amex Platinum Card

I used my Amex Platinum's Q3 Lululemon statement credit for a black Steady State SuperLoft Crew shirt. Although it’s designed for men, this sweatshirt fits me exceptionally well.

Lululemon also offers a women's version of this, if you'd prefer a different fit. I currently plan to use my Q4 statement credit to buy another of these shirts in a different color.

TPG credit cards writer Stephanie Stevens is a huge fan of the clear version of the Everywhere Belt Bag.

She feels the bag is great for stadiums or events with clear-bag policies. Best of all, it is reasonably priced and makes a great gift.

Buying two bags for $76 would use your full $75 quarterly statement credit, leaving you with just $1 to pay (before applicable taxes). You could also buy one bag and put the remaining credit toward another eligible purchase.

Buy: Everywhere Belt Bag 1L Clear for $38

TPG's lead writer for loyalty programs, Katie Genter, recently used her statement credit on this hoodie. It comes in three different basic color options, making it easy to pair with a variety of outfits.

If you're someone who gets cold easily while traveling, this hoodie could be a great item to throw on during your flight, train ride or car ride. The Amex Platinum's up to $75 quarterly Lululemon statement credit brings the total cost down to just $23.

Katie also noted that she used a statement credit from a different quarter to purchase this long-sleeve shirt. This is a soft, casual shirt that can work for a relaxed day around the house, a long travel day or as a casual top for a day of sightseeing.

Keep in mind that this item is marked Final Sale, so you won't be able to return it online if it doesn't fit or otherwise meet your expectations. However, your Amex Platinum's shopping protections should be usable here if your item arrives damaged or not as described. Alternatively, you may be able to return it in-store for store credit.

Buy: All Yours Organic Cotton-Blend Long-Sleeve Shirt for $29

I used my up to $75 Lululemon statement credit for Q1 2026 on a pair of these joggers. They're incredibly soft and feel high-quality.

If you're looking for a comfortable pair of joggers to throw on after work or for a light workout, these pants are hard to beat. (This is a Final Sale item.)

Buy: Heavyweight Soft Jersey Relaxed Fit Jogger for $69

TPG senior analyst Jared Nord noted that, while he already has one of these hoodies, he may pick up another, given that the price is currently within the threshold for the Amex Platinum's up to $75 quarterly Lululemon statement credit.

This hoodie is available in a wide range of colors, making it easy to find a color you like. As with some other items mentioned, this is marked Final Sale.

Buy: Smooth Spacer Classic-Fit Pullover Hoodie for $69 in select colors; regular price $138

TPG's managing editor for credit cards, Giselle Gomez, bought this item earlier this quarter. She "found them to be super comfortable for traveling," and added she "might circle back and get them in another color."

The price for these pants varies, so make sure to pay close attention to the total amount when adding your color choice to your cart. Depending on the color you choose, your Amex Platinum's quarterly up-to-$75 Lululemon statement credit may not cover the entire purchase.

Buy: Groove Nulu High-Rise Flared Pant Regular $59 in select colors; regular price $118

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $75 in Lululemon statement credits each quarter. If you shop at the retailer only once and spend less than $75, you’ll forfeit any unused portion of the statement credit when the next quarter begins.

To maximize this benefit, first make sure you’re enrolled in the statement credit, then click through a shopping portal before making your purchase. While you’ll earn only 1 point per dollar spent with your Platinum Card, you may be able to pick up additional rewards through a shopping portal. (At the time of publication, Rakuten is not offering rewards on Lululemon purchases.)

Next, aim to use the full $75 statement credit each quarter. You don’t have to spend it all in a single transaction, and you can spread your purchases across multiple orders if needed. Since many popular Lululemon items — including jackets, pants and shirts — cost more than $75, using the entire statement credit shouldn’t be difficult.

If you buy an item you’re not happy with, consider exchanging it instead of returning it. A return could trigger a statement credit reversal, and you may not be able to use your statement credit again during that quarter.

You can also stretch your statement credit further by purchasing sale items. (Note that purchases made at Lululemon outlet locations don’t qualify.)

Finally, don’t wait until the last minute to use your quarterly statement credit. If your purchase doesn’t post before the end of the quarter, it could trigger the following quarter’s statement credit instead.

Related: Forgettable statement credits checklist: Perks and benefits not to be overlooked

The Lululemon statement credit on the Amex Platinum is a great benefit for those who enjoy the brand. Consider these TPG-recommended items, or, if you already have your own favorites, be sure to purchase them using your Amex Platinum next time.

Don't forget to use your Q4 Lululemon statement credit, since you don't want to leave that value on the table.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum.

#6161. Hotel CEOs Reveal Where They Think Travel Is Headed—But AI Could Make Them Lower Room Prices

GHA Discovery asked hotel CEOs what will shape their business over the next few years, and 87% expect AI assistants to be among the most important booking channels by 2030. They expect hotel websites and loyalty programs to matter more than online travel agencies. Hotels would love to stop paying commissions to Expedia and Booking.com. But I think they’re overlooking how much harder a sufficiently capable AI will make it to charge customers more than they need to pay. Hotels may get more direct bookings while earning less from each guest booking direct. The short GHA Hotel Brand CEO Outlook 2027 is worth reading. GHA Discovery connects about 60 brands and 1,000 hotels, including Kempinski, Anantara, Capella, Pan Pacific, NH and smaller groups like Lore. I think the program gets far less attention than it deserves and I’ve had some fantastic stays. What Hotel CEOs Expect This was an August survey of 30 CEOs from GHA brands: They’re worried, but still expect growth. 90% named geopolitical instability among their biggest challenges over the next five years. Nearly half expect like-for-like hotel revenue to grow at least 5% in 2027. (Notably, GHA itself is based in Dubai.) International leisure travel is the growth engine. 73% expect international demand to outperform domestic, and 90% expect international leisure travel to increase. India is almost as widely cited as the United States. 53% named the U.S. as a source of international growth, versus 50% for India and 40% each for China and the U.K. AI is expected to dominate hotel discovery. For influence on bookings in 2030, AI assistants scored 87%, hotel websites and apps 50%, loyalty platforms 47%, and online travel agencies 30%. Loyalty matters, and recognition leads their list of differentiators. 83% consider loyalty critical or very important to revenue growth. Recognition was selected by 70% as a factor distinguishing successful programs, versus 57% for personalization and 47% for rewards. India is significant, a small share of a very large population crossing the income threshold for international travel produces a lot of customers. India had 32.83 million departures by Indian nationals in 2025, up 6.3%. And the number of people there worth more than $30 million grew 63% between 2021 and 2026. The opportunity comes from the number of people who can afford to travel, rather than population numbers themselves. The finding in the report I’m skeptical of is only 13% selecting price as a leading influence on hotel decisions in 2030. Unless money just no longer matters in a post-AGI world (!) this seems implausible. Hotel brand also scored just 13%, compared with 43% for loyalty benefits. An AI recommendation can be based on price. Putting “AI recommendations” and “price” in separate buckets doesn’t establish that price stops mattering to the AI. Hotels Can Lose Pricing Power Even As More Guests Book Direct Online travel agencies do two things that hotels value. They bring customers. Someone may not know the hotel exists, may not have a preferred chain, or may want to compare properties across chains. Expedia, Booking.com and others supply an audience the hotel doesn’t reach on its own. They help hotels charge different customers different prices. A hotel wants to sell rooms that would otherwise sit empty without cutting the price for everyone who would’ve paid more. Packages, restricted membership rates and opaque offers can let them discount without putting the same lower rate on their own site. I’ve written about how hotels distribute discounted inventory outside their public rates, and why a card travel portal can sometimes beat the hotel’s own member price. Booking direct isn’t automatically the cheapest option. The hotel has room to be more generous when it isn’t spending on the OTA commission. It can give some of that money to the guest as a lower price, rewards or benefits. The agency has its own operating costs and profit to cover. It seems like a chain could undercut the third party. But today’s room rate isn’t fixed while AI just redistributes the savings. If AI can find the right small hotel even though I’ve never heard of it, that’s less reason to start with Expedia and more reason to book direct. But it’s also less reason to pay a premium for the familiar hotel I would’ve booked without doing much research. And where there are opaque offers the AI may find those too. It could ask several suitable hotels for their best offer, comparing cash discounts with credits and benefits, and without my needing to spend time negotiating. This already matters in my own choices. In Venice, I wanted a location that worked for my family, rather than staying on Murano just to use Hyatt. At NH Collection Palazzo dei Dogi, GHA status helped me with early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout. An assistant that knows my family’s needs can compare that entire package against the alternatives. It can consider a different neighborhood, a different destination, or different dates, rather than just finding another website selling the same room. It can also work through offers that are currently tedious to find. Opaque hotels become less opaque if the assistant can identify them from their amenities, location and photos. Still, knowing about a corporate rate doesn’t make you eligible for it. I’d expect pressure on direct booking margins because consumers have the intelligence in their pockets that just solved math. They may avoid OTA commissions but get rates competed down, and while lower commissions apply only to a limited piece of their business, the lower rates would affect the entire hotel. An unknown hotel may gain enough customers to come out well ahead. A unique property on a sold out night has pricing power. But more direct bookings may or may not mean greater profits. Recognition Doesn’t Replace Rewards The report’s loyalty finding interests me because I’ve been writing about recognition and reward as the twin pillars of loyalty for more than a decade. They’re different things, and a good program does both. Recognition can be the thing a traveler values most. But if getting it means giving up the rebate they’d earn elsewhere, they’re actually having to pay for that recognition. A guest may care more about their treatment but that’s holding rewards constant. GHA addressed this when it relaunched Discovery in December 2021. Previously, it offered status benefits and Local Experience awards. Those awards could be great, but a business traveler working all day often had no use for the experience on offer. Discovery Dollars gave members a flexible rebate they could put toward a hotel bill. The CEO survey asks what will differentiate successful programs. That’s compatible with rewards being something customers already expect. It doesn’t mean you can take the rewards away. And in GHA’s separate research among more than 9,000 members this year, generosity was the leading program attribute. Ease of earning and spending Discovery Dollars and hotel benefits both rated highly. Why I Value GHA Discovery I’ve called GHA my second favorite hotel loyalty program, after Hyatt. Hyatt still has the advantages of confirmed suites at booking, guaranteed late checkout at most properties and a more consistent breakfast benefit. GHA gives me interesting hotels where I still receive real benefits. At Riggs in Washington, D.C., I wound up in the suite that used to be the bank’s boardroom, with a dining table for 12. I’d booked through Chase’s The Edit and stacked its benefits with GHA status. At Kempinski Cancun, I combined American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts with GHA and received an oceanfront suite and club access. Members earn 4% to 7% back in Discovery Dollars on eligible spending, depending on status. One Discovery Dollar is worth one U.S. dollar toward eligible spending at participating hotels. Titanium earns 7%, with those regularly earned dollars valid for 24 months. Promotional dollars can expire sooner. Titanium includes a two-category upgrade, 11 a.m. early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout, subject to availability. Breakfast for two is included at participating brands on direct bookings. You can earn Titanium with 30 eligible nights, $15,000 in eligible spending, or stays at three qualifying brands in a calendar year. The last route can mean just three one-night stays (NH Hotels, NH Collection and nhow count together as one brand). At the Lyle in D.C., the staff arranged fresh coffee for me at 5 a.m., two hours before room service opened. It arrived at exactly 5 a.m. That’s the sort of thing I remember and go back for. I’ve also covered their unusually accessible status matches. The current offer runs through November 30, 2026, with approved status lasting through December 31, 2027: Platinum: $100 application fee, with D$50 back. Titanium: $150 application fee, with D$75 back. There’s no stay challenge. Hilton Diamond, Hyatt Globalist, Marriott Platinum and above, and IHG Platinum and above are among the statuses that match to Titanium. Eligible airline and cruise status, and some credit cards, qualify too. The gift dollars expire after 12 months, and the terms allow only one GHA status match. For someone with an upcoming stay at one of these hotels, $150 with $75 back in hotel spending can be a very good way to get treated better. I’d like my future travel assistant to notice that before it tells me I’ve saved $20 booking the same hotel without benefits through Expedia. You can earn Titanium with 30 eligible nights, $15,000 in eligible spending, or stays at three qualifying brands in a calendar year. The last route can mean just three one-night stays (NH Hotels, NH Collection and nhow count together as one brand). At the Lyle in D.C., the staff arranged fresh coffee for me at 5 a.m., two hours before room service opened. It arrived at exactly 5 a.m. That’s the sort of thing I remember and go back for. I’ve also covered their unusually accessible status matches. The current offer runs through November 30, 2026, with approved status lasting through December 31, 2027: Platinum: $100 application fee, with D$50 back. Titanium: $150 application fee, with D$75 back. There’s no stay challenge. Hilton Diamond, Hyatt Globalist, Marriott Platinum and above, and IHG Platinum and above are among the statuses that match to Titanium. Eligible airline and cruise status, and some credit cards, qualify too. The gift dollars expire after 12 months, and the terms allow only one GHA status match. For someone with an upcoming stay at one of these hotels, $150 with $75 back in hotel spending can be a very good way to get treated better. Online travel agencies do two things that hotels value.

I’ve written about how hotels distribute discounted inventory outside their public rates, and why a card travel portal can sometimes beat the hotel’s own member price. Booking direct isn’t automatically the cheapest option.

The hotel has room to be more generous when it isn’t spending on the OTA commission. It can give some of that money to the guest as a lower price, rewards or benefits. The agency has its own operating costs and profit to cover. It seems like a chain could undercut the third party. But today’s room rate isn’t fixed while AI just redistributes the savings.

If AI can find the right small hotel even though I’ve never heard of it, that’s less reason to start with Expedia and more reason to book direct. But it’s also less reason to pay a premium for the familiar hotel I would’ve booked without doing much research. And where there are opaque offers the AI may find those too. It could ask several suitable hotels for their best offer, comparing cash discounts with credits and benefits, and without my needing to spend time negotiating.

This already matters in my own choices. In Venice, I wanted a location that worked for my family, rather than staying on Murano just to use Hyatt. At NH Collection Palazzo dei Dogi, GHA status helped me with early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout.

An assistant that knows my family’s needs can compare that entire package against the alternatives. It can consider a different neighborhood, a different destination, or different dates, rather than just finding another website selling the same room.

It can also work through offers that are currently tedious to find. Opaque hotels become less opaque if the assistant can identify them from their amenities, location and photos. Still, knowing about a corporate rate doesn’t make you eligible for it.

I’d expect pressure on direct booking margins because consumers have the intelligence in their pockets that just solved math. They may avoid OTA commissions but get rates competed down, and while lower commissions apply only to a limited piece of their business, the lower rates would affect the entire hotel. An unknown hotel may gain enough customers to come out well ahead. A unique property on a sold out night has pricing power. But more direct bookings may or may not mean greater profits.

The report’s loyalty finding interests me because I’ve been writing about recognition and reward as the twin pillars of loyalty for more than a decade. They’re different things, and a good program does both. Recognition can be the thing a traveler values most. But if getting it means giving up the rebate they’d earn elsewhere, they’re actually having to pay for that recognition. A guest may care more about their treatment but that’s holding rewards constant. GHA addressed this when it relaunched Discovery in December 2021. Previously, it offered status benefits and Local Experience awards. Those awards could be great, but a business traveler working all day often had no use for the experience on offer. Discovery Dollars gave members a flexible rebate they could put toward a hotel bill. The CEO survey asks what will differentiate successful programs. That’s compatible with rewards being something customers already expect. It doesn’t mean you can take the rewards away. And in GHA’s separate research among more than 9,000 members this year, generosity was the leading program attribute. Ease of earning and spending Discovery Dollars and hotel benefits both rated highly. Why I Value GHA Discovery I’ve called GHA my second favorite hotel loyalty program, after Hyatt. Hyatt still has the advantages of confirmed suites at booking, guaranteed late checkout at most properties and a more consistent breakfast benefit. GHA gives me interesting hotels where I still receive real benefits. At Riggs in Washington, D.C., I wound up in the suite that used to be the bank’s boardroom, with a dining table for 12. I’d booked through Chase’s The Edit and stacked its benefits with GHA status. At Kempinski Cancun, I combined American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts with GHA and received an oceanfront suite and club access. I was not quite sure what this article was about. Is it about GHA? You were right in a previous post, I know little about it. Maybe I should find out.

If it is about booking directly, Nike’s attempt to force everyone to buy their shoes directly was a disaster. Booking engines provide visibility, even to major brands. I still use Agoda to book in Asia, even though it is now owned by Booking Holdings. For small hotels, like a nice family hotel with dinky clean rooms I stayed in Tokyo or the great one bedroom suite with a free breakfast in Phnom Penh, Agoda opens up a world market.

If it about AI, AI might help. However, (1) My iphone AI news app has decided that I want to read food and recipe, celerity, puzzles. I cannot figure out how to turn off the feed of crap stories. (2) My Youtube app has decided to push a steady stream of AI generated content, that mostly is taken from Wikipedia and shorts. I cannot seem to turn it off, so I turned off all suggestions and search. (3) My Netflicks app has decided I like Korean movies (I have no idea why), and sends me pages of suggestions. I cannot get it to stop. It gives me a headache, and I don’t watch anything. I might cancel Netflicks (4) Don’t get me started about customer service AI. Until I see AI working in my own life, I am naturally skeptical that AI will solve my hotel choices any time soon.

The main problem is incentives. Hotel operators actual customers are not guests; it’s property owners. Rarely do these corporations own the underlying real estate. So, they don’t really care about consumers so much as shareholders, property owners, and their own executive compensation. Fix the incentives; magically, consumers will be treated better. At the very least, better guardrails to protect from outright fraud, deceptive practices, please.

Yeah, just charge a resort fee and for parking in the middle of Nebraska hotels.

This article is clearly a pitch for GHA, which quite frankly, is lame. Pass.

@Gene — What is it with Gary (and Ben) promoting GHA?! Like, never heard of it before these guys… bah!

#6160. Citi AAdvantage Business Card 75K Bonus Miles Offer (Double Dip Loyalty Points!)

The Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® is American’s primary co-branded business credit card. We’ve just seen an excellent new limited time welcome offer rolled out on the card, which is in line with the highest ever offer that we’ve seen on the card.

That makes this the ideal time to apply. Not only that, but this is a card that many people will want, given that it’s my favorite American card for earning AAdvantage elite status, since you can basically double dip Loyalty Points.

Link: Learn more about the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard®

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card currently has a limited time welcome offer of 75,000 AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $5,000 within the first five months. This is a highest-ever offer, in line with the best bonuses I recall seeing on the card.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value AAdvantage miles at 1.5 cents each, so to me the bonus is worth $1,125. There are some incredible uses of American AAdvantage miles, including for travel on some world class partner airlines.

Also keep in mind that credit card spending will qualify for Loyalty Points (helping you earn elite status, including Gold, Platinum, Platinum Pro, or Executive Platinum), though the welcome bonus as such won’t. Upon completing minimum spending, you’d earn a minimum of 5,000 Loyalty Points. As I’ll explain below, you can even double dip the Loyalty Points you earn.

If you’re interested in applying for the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, the typical Citi credit card application restrictions apply, including that you can be approved for at most one Citi card every eight days, and at most two Citi cards every 65 days.

On top of that, the bonus isn’t available to those who have received a new account bonus on this exact card in the past 48 months. Eligibility is unrelated to having any other American Airlines credit cards.

If you’re concerned about Chase’s 5/24 rule, note that applying for a Citi business card generally won’t count toward that limit. I should also mention that at least anecdotally, this card seems to be quite easy to get approved for.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card has an annual fee that’s waived for the first year, so you can “try” the card before you have to pay a fee. While the fee after that is technically still $99, it’s increasing to $150 as of January 24, 2027, so that’s what you’d pay on account renewal.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers a variety of valuable perks, including:

Above I mentioned how the Citi AAdvantage Business Card is the best card for earning AAdvantage elite status. The reason is because through December 31, 2028, the card essentially lets you double dip Loyalty Points. If you add an authorized user, their spending will earn 1x Loyalty Points per dollar spent for both their own account, and for the primary cardmember’s account. So this is a way to essentially get two-for-one elite status qualification, which is awesome.

With the annual fee increasing as of January 2027, the card will also pick up several valuable new perks, including the following:

Read a detailed review of the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus of 75,000 AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $5,000 within the first five months. This is a great offer on a valuable card that even has its annual fee waived for the first year.

This is also my favorite card for earning AAdvantage elite status, since you can essentially earn Loyalty Points for two members at once. Authorized user spending earns Loyalty Points for the authorized user’s AAdvantage account, and also for the primary cardmember’s AAdvantage account.

Anyone plan to pick up the Citi AAdvantage Business Card with 75K miles?

#6158. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

#6156. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

#6155. Air Serbia Flight Turns Back As Spy Onboard Accused Of Bypassing Security

An Air Serbia flight to Moscow made it as far as Lithuania before turning around and flying back to Belgrade, where everyone had to get off and go through security again. Reportedly Serbia’s former intelligence chief was allowed to board without completing security screening. He says he’s being targeted by political opponents. The flight eventually reached Moscow about seven hours late, with spy master Aleksandar Vulin still onboard. Flight JU134 departed Belgrade at 6:48 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3. The Airbus A320, registration YU-APH, turned back over southern Lithuania and landed back in Belgrade at 9:56 p.m. That’s more than three hours of flying to end up where passengers started. Flightradar24 tracks Air Serbia flight JU134 returning to Belgrade after turning around over Lithuania. Also onboard were Dušan Bajatović, who runs state gas company Srbijagas, and politician Nenad Popović. Bajatović. Everyone and their luggage went through another inspection. Passengers reboarded shortly before 2 a.m., and a replacement crew took over because of duty time limits. According to Belgrade’s Third Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office: Police contacted the duty prosecutor at 8:26 p.m. They described a passenger passing through the security area with an officer from Serbia’s intelligence agency without the required screening. A police memo received the next day added that the passenger had triggered an alarm and hadn’t received the additional inspection. Radio audio circulated by Serbian media includes the captain telling passengers the return was for security reasons, along with instructions to the crew after landing. Radio communication from the return of Air Serbia flight JU134, shared by journalist Žarko Bogosavljević. Vulin denies wrongdoing. He says he slept through the flight, woke up back in Belgrade, and found police waiting. His account includes asking them, “Colleagues, have you come for me?” He says they laughed and told him they hadn’t. He says he passed the checks, nothing illegal was found, and the whole thing was an attempt to impress the country’s incoming political leadership. His stated reason for going to Moscow was to seek an extension of Serbia’s gas agreement with Russia. He subsequently posted from Moscow denying that he’d fled Serbia. Aleksandar Vulin’s response after arriving in Moscow. Vulin has been Serbia’s defense minister, interior minister, intelligence chief and deputy prime minister. The United States sanctioned him in 2023, alleging corruption and assistance to Russian influence operations. His political ally Aleksandar Vučić’s side lost Serbia’s October 25 election. I’ve covered an American Airlines Charlotte–Cancun flight that returned after a former airline employee bypassed screening, so returning a flight over an unscreened passenger isn’t unique to Serbia. Here, though, the aircraft was much farther along. Returning to the airport that identified the problem puts the passenger, the screeners and the surveillance records under the same authorities. And it may be difficult (and embarrassing) to coordinate with a closer airport in another country to handle this and without the airline’s same presence on the ground. Belgrade’s prosecutor’s office is now seeking answers from the airport’s security director, including who ordered the return, what security assessment supported it, whether procedures were violated before departure, and who authorized the flight to leave again. #6153. Transfer Citi ThankYou Points To Turkish Miles&Smiles With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

At the moment, it’s possible to earn up to a 40% bonus when you transfer Citi ThankYou points to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, the bonus isn’t being offered on Citi’s end, but instead, is being offered on Turkish Airlines’ end.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from the Citi ThankYou program in the United States to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, there are some important terms to be aware of:

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,400 Miles&Smiles miles for every 1,000 Citi ThankYou points transferred, though only after the fact.

There are several great cards earning Citi ThankYou points, including the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) and Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (learn more), and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Back in the day, the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles program offered incredible redemption values across the board, but that’s no longer really the case. At this point, I’d say the sweet spot with the Miles&Smiles program is if you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines specifically to or from Istanbul.

That’s because the Miles&Smiles program now charges per segment for awards on Turkish Airlines metal. You can find the cost of one-way saver awards below, just to give you a sense of pricing.

So as an example, a one-way business class award between the United States and Istanbul will cost you 65,000 miles. In other words, with a 40% transfer bonus, you’d be paying around 47,000 Citi ThankYou points for a business class award, which is a pretty great deal.

If you know what you’re doing and have specific redemption plans in mind, this could be a great deal. Just be sure you understand the complexities of the program, and read my guide to the Turkish Miles&Smiles program. Also keep in mind the Miles&Smiles expiration policy, which is that miles expire at the end of the third year after which they’re earned, regardless of activity.

The other big restriction is that the bonus miles will only post after the campaign is done, so you couldn’t transfer points and then immediately redeem all of them (including the bonus). The cap on 50,000 bonus miles is also limiting. But hey, if you value Turkish miles, this could definitely offer some value.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. The catch is that the bonus miles only post after the end of the campaign, and you can only earn 50,000 bonus miles with this offer.

If you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines to or from Istanbul, there are some good deals to be had by taking advantage of this.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this transfer bonus from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles?

Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday, a stunning reversal just two days before Michigan voters decide one of the countryâs closely watched Senate races.
