#6136. Southwest’s New Platinum Status Adds Too Little—10 Ways Rapid Rewards Should Fix Its New Program

Southwest Airlines is adding Platinum status to Rapid Rewards, but someone who already has A-List Preferred and Companion Pass won’t get much new. A third checked bag, earlier boarding, and a higher advertised earning bonus (offset by lower base-earning on higher fares) are very modest additions considering they’re launching a new top tier. Gold, the replacement for A-List Preferred, already gets the same seats. The 2027 overhaul makes things simpler by unifying qualification for elite status and Companion Pass. And they’re adding award travel on Icelandair, China Airlines and Etihad Airways beginning in the spring, including in premium cabins. We don’t yet know redemption pricing, rules or surcharges, so we don’t know how much value those will deliver. I’ve argued that Southwest’s changes follow from one another. Broader distribution puts their fares alongside everyone else’s. That creates pressure to unbundle with basic economy and paid seats and bags. Selling better seats requires assigned seating. Once they’ve given up the old differences, they need more of the benefits that make other airlines worth choosing. Southwest is inexorably becoming like the rest of the industry, but – they insist – with friendler crews. They at least need to become like everyone else without offering less. I offered ten ways to improve Rapid Rewards in 2022. Some, including partner airline redemptions and stronger credit card earning toward status, are finally being addressed. Here’s what I’d do next. Deliver Elite Members’ Bags First Southwest baggage delivery can be slow. That was easier to tolerate when checking bags was free for everyone. Once they’re charging for the service, standing around a carousel feels different. They should offer priority baggage handling for elites, with Gold and Platinum bags among the first delivered. This requires actually sorting and loading the bags so they come out first, not just a colored tag. And back it with a delivery guarantee. Delta offers 2,500 miles when checked bags take more than 20 minutes from gate arrival to the carousel. Alaska has a similar guarantee (and was actually first). Southwest could start with a guarantee for its top elites. I’d rather get my first bag promptly than have a free third one. Give Platinum Members Priority For An Empty Middle SeatSouthwest doesn’t have first class upgrades to offer. It can still make sitting in coach better. When a Platinum member selects a window or aisle in a regular legroom row, hold the adjacent middle seat out of routine seat assignments until it’s needed. Keep selling the flight, and release the seat at the gate if passengers need it. This would determine who gets the empty seat when a flight isn’t full. Someone is going to have extra space beside them. Give the customer who earned the highest status the best chance of being that person. Limiting this to ordinary coach would avoid taking some premium seats they’re trying to sell out of inventory. An empty middle can be better than a few additional inches of legroom. Introduce Lifetime Elite StatusAmerican, Delta, United and Alaska all recognize lifetime flying. Southwest now should, too. I’d base on miles or flight segments since Southwest has never had a long haul netowrk to rack up 20,000 flown miles on a roundtrip. For instance, 1,000 one-way trips could earn lifetime Silver, 2,000 could earn lifetime Gold, and 3,000 lifetime Platinum. I don’t know whether Southwest has the database to support historical flying like this. Give Elites An Award Rebate Make points worth more to the customers who earn status. A 10% rebate on Southwest awards for Gold and 15% for Platinum would make their points more valuable, and could be more easily managed than an award discount. Some Southwest credit cards already provide annual 10% or 15% discount codes. This is especially important because the new program cuts earning on expensive fares. As I laid out in comparing the new tiers, a Choice Extra ticket earns an A-List Preferred member 28 points per eligible dollar today, versus 22 for a Platinum member next year. Let Families Pool Points Free Southwest sells family travel and has one of the best benefits for traveling with someone else. Yet its program rules prohibit members from pooling points. Let a household combine its balances without paying a transfer fee. You can already use your points to book someone else’s ticket. The problem is having enough points across several accounts, but not enough in any one account for the award you want. JetBlue has offered free pooling for groups of up to seven people for years. United has family accounts, and this is a big feature in international progams. Count Award Flights Toward Status A flight paid for entirely with Rapid Rewards points doesn’t count as a qualifying flight. Southwest should change that, like Delta and Alaska do, and include partner awards as that part of the program develops. Southwest wants people to earn points from its credit cards and partners, then use them to fly. Treating that journey as less valuable to the airline makes no sense. Make Companion Pass More Useful When Traveling With Different People Companion Pass remains Southwest’s strongest benefit. But the new program keeps the old restrictions: one designated companion at a time, three changes per calendar year, and existing companion reservations must be canceled before switching people. Let Platinum members designate a small group, perhaps three people, and choose one companion for each trip. A spouse on one trip, a child on another. Still one companion per flight, still traveling with the member, with limits on changing the roster. I’d also let Platinum members use Companion Pass for an adjacent empty seat when traveling alone, an idea I included in my earlier wishlist. This would be a confirmed seat reservation, consuming inventory just as a companion booking does. A member whose travel is mostly business shouldn’t need to bring another person on the trip to get substantial value from the program’s biggest reward. Allow Confirmed Same-Day Changes On Basic Fares Southwest already lets elites use their seating benefits on Basic. That’s a real advantage over competitors, and it extends to family members on the same reservation. But even the new Platinum tier won’t receive free confirmed same-day changes on Basic. Members can stand by. They need to buy Choice or higher to confirm the change without paying a fare difference. Give Gold and Platinum confirmed changes into available seats on the day of travel, regardless of their original fare. Keep the same origin and destination, and let the member choose an available itinerary that gets them there sooner or works better with their schedule. Southwest already provides the service on more expensive fares, here earned status would supply it. Make Southwest Status Useful On Its Airline Partners The international redemption announcement addresses not being able to use Southwest points for long haul travel. The awards need solid pricing and inventory. I expect that we’ll eventually see reciprocal status recognition, but that needs to come quickly: priority check-in, baggage allowances, boarding and seat benefits and lounge access would make Gold and Platinum valuable even when member travels beyond Southwest’s route map. Give Platinum A Choice Of Benefits Southwest is building Icon Lounges, with openings planned to begin in late 2027. Access has been announced through a forthcoming premium Chase card. They haven’t announced a Platinum lounge benefit. Give members an annual choice when they earn Platinum: perhaps some lounge passes which could encourage them to try the product and get the card, or to share the passes with others. They might choose a travel credit or certificates that let friends and family select extra legroom seats when the member isn’t traveling. Southwest is already introducing two milestones, at 20,000 and 95,000 qualifying points which are below Platinum. The earlier milestone’s Preferred seat certificates aren’t extra legroom upgrades and can’t be gifted, so certificates for a friend to choose a better seat would add something different. They should continue with milestones above platinum, and continue offering choice benefits. Southwest Airlines is remaking itself in the image of the rest of the airline industry – with the same kinds of restrictions, but also adding many of the same amenities. They will have three elite tiers, but those tiers need to be competitive. I want Southwest to succeed. Are these things that would do it for you? What’s missing from my list? The 2027 overhaul makes things simpler by unifying qualification for elite status and Companion Pass. And they’re adding award travel on Icelandair, China Airlines and Etihad Airways beginning in the spring, including in premium cabins. We don’t yet know redemption pricing, rules or surcharges, so we don’t know how much value those will deliver.

I’ve argued that Southwest’s changes follow from one another. Broader distribution puts their fares alongside everyone else’s. That creates pressure to unbundle with basic economy and paid seats and bags. Selling better seats requires assigned seating. Once they’ve given up the old differences, they need more of the benefits that make other airlines worth choosing.

Southwest is inexorably becoming like the rest of the industry, but – they insist – with friendler crews. They at least need to become like everyone else without offering less.

I offered ten ways to improve Rapid Rewards in 2022. Some, including partner airline redemptions and stronger credit card earning toward status, are finally being addressed. Here’s what I’d do next.

Deliver Elite Members’ Bags First Southwest baggage delivery can be slow. That was easier to tolerate when checking bags was free for everyone. Once they’re charging for the service, standing around a carousel feels different.

They should offer priority baggage handling for elites, with Gold and Platinum bags among the first delivered. This requires actually sorting and loading the bags so they come out first, not just a colored tag. And back it with a delivery guarantee. Delta offers 2,500 miles when checked bags take more than 20 minutes from gate arrival to the carousel. Alaska has a similar guarantee (and was actually first). Southwest could start with a guarantee for its top elites. I’d rather get my first bag promptly than have a free third one.

Give Platinum Members Priority For An Empty Middle SeatSouthwest doesn’t have first class upgrades to offer. It can still make sitting in coach better.

When a Platinum member selects a window or aisle in a regular legroom row, hold the adjacent middle seat out of routine seat assignments until it’s needed. Keep selling the flight, and release the seat at the gate if passengers need it. This would determine who gets the empty seat when a flight isn’t full. Someone is going to have extra space beside them. Give the customer who earned the highest status the best chance of being that person.

Limiting this to ordinary coach would avoid taking some premium seats they’re trying to sell out of inventory. An empty middle can be better than a few additional inches of legroom.

Introduce Lifetime Elite StatusAmerican, Delta, United and Alaska all recognize lifetime flying. Southwest now should, too.

I’d base on miles or flight segments since Southwest has never had a long haul netowrk to rack up 20,000 flown miles on a roundtrip. For instance, 1,000 one-way trips could earn lifetime Silver, 2,000 could earn lifetime Gold, and 3,000 lifetime Platinum. I don’t know whether Southwest has the database to support historical flying like this.

This is especially important because the new program cuts earning on expensive fares. As I laid out in comparing the new tiers, a Choice Extra ticket earns an A-List Preferred member 28 points per eligible dollar today, versus 22 for a Platinum member next year.

Let Families Pool Points Free Southwest sells family travel and has one of the best benefits for traveling with someone else. Yet its program rules prohibit members from pooling points. Let a household combine its balances without paying a transfer fee. You can already use your points to book someone else’s ticket. The problem is having enough points across several accounts, but not enough in any one account for the award you want.

JetBlue has offered free pooling for groups of up to seven people for years. United has family accounts, and this is a big feature in international progams.

Count Award Flights Toward Status A flight paid for entirely with Rapid Rewards points doesn’t count as a qualifying flight. Southwest should change that, like Delta and Alaska do, and include partner awards as that part of the program develops.

Southwest wants people to earn points from its credit cards and partners, then use them to fly. Treating that journey as less valuable to the airline makes no sense.

Let Platinum members designate a small group, perhaps three people, and choose one companion for each trip. A spouse on one trip, a child on another. Still one companion per flight, still traveling with the member, with limits on changing the roster. I’d also let Platinum members use Companion Pass for an adjacent empty seat when traveling alone, an idea I included in my earlier wishlist. This would be a confirmed seat reservation, consuming inventory just as a companion booking does. A member whose travel is mostly business shouldn’t need to bring another person on the trip to get substantial value from the program’s biggest reward. Allow Confirmed Same-Day Changes On Basic Fares Southwest already lets elites use their seating benefits on Basic. That’s a real advantage over competitors, and it extends to family members on the same reservation. But even the new Platinum tier won’t receive free confirmed same-day changes on Basic. Members can stand by. They need to buy Choice or higher to confirm the change without paying a fare difference. Give Gold and Platinum confirmed changes into available seats on the day of travel, regardless of their original fare. Keep the same origin and destination, and let the member choose an available itinerary that gets them there sooner or works better with their schedule. Southwest already provides the service on more expensive fares, here earned status would supply it. Make Southwest Status Useful On Its Airline Partners The international redemption announcement addresses not being able to use Southwest points for long haul travel. The awards need solid pricing and inventory. I expect that we’ll eventually see reciprocal status recognition, but that needs to come quickly: priority check-in, baggage allowances, boarding and seat benefits and lounge access would make Gold and Platinum valuable even when member travels beyond Southwest’s route map. So what you’re saying is that if I spend $75k on the CSR I can get the amazing benefits that come with Southwest A-List / Silver status?

>Count Award Flights Toward Status Southwest has done this a couple times in past years. It makes sense because Southwest has been paid for the points and Southwest recognizes revenue when they are flown.

>Introduce Lifetime Elite Status I would like to think my 2000+ flights count for something, even though I know they don’t.

>Allow Confirmed Same-Day Changes On Basic Fares This would be great but it won’t happen because it would reduce revenue by up to 50% on short haul trips booked in advance. Southwest has fired its loyal low-fare customers and does not want to re-hire them.

One improvement unrelated to elite status would be to eliminate or somehow mitigate expiration of travel funds. I have been booking on points to avoid having to worry about funds expiration. If funds expiration were eliminated I would have booked those flights on cash fares. I believe that Southwest is foolish to count breakage as revenue without accurately estimating how many cash fare sales are lost because of funds expiration.

Do they fly DC to Shreveport? Asking for a frenemy who has a lawn business he needs to get back to…

Also, do they fly from Beverly Hills to Miami? I presume Bill Maher will soon move to Florida, as well. (Oh, and gonna need a direct from Rochester Hills, Michigan, to Florida, or Tel Aviv, you know, for Haley and her fiancé.)

We have companion thru end of 2027. After that we’ll cancel our SW credit card and focus on United. No point in sticking with, as even the planned international partnerships are of no interest. My spouse has been ALP for over 15 years. I’ve had Companion for over 10. There’s really no place SWA goes that other airlines don’t that we need to get to.

#6135. Park Hyatt Riviera Maya Cancun, Brand’s First All-Inclusive, Opens Soon

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

In late 2023, Hyatt and Parks Hospitality Holdings announced a collaboration that will expand Hyatt’s footprint in Mexico, with the development of four new properties. If you ask me, the most interesting of these is the new Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, which will also be the brand’s first all-inclusive property.

There’s now an update, as the hotel’s opening date has just been moved forward by a couple of months, and it’s now expected to open in the coming weeks.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, located in Cancun, Mexico, is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 3, 2026. The hotel was initially supposed to open in 2025, then it started accepting reservations for stays as of February 2027, and now it’s accepting reservations for stays as of late 2026.

Hopefully the current opening date sticks, but if you book in the first several months the hotel is open, don’t be surprised if we see an additional delay, or at least don’t be surprised if not everything is ready.

The 148-key property will have a first-ever concept for the Park Hyatt brand, as it will be all-inclusive. Admittedly this is pretty normal for the Cancun area, but still, it’s noteworthy for a brand like Park Hyatt.

Hyatt has been leaning heavily into the all-inclusive space in recent times, particularly through acquisitions. So while Hyatt has grown massively in terms of its number of all-inclusive brands, it’s surprising to see even a traditionally non all-inclusive brand get this kind of an experience.

I’m generally not a fan of all-inclusives, or at least historically haven’t chosen to vacation at them. However, after my recent Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection cruise, there is something I really enjoyed about not being nickel-and-dimed for everything, given how expensive luxury hospitality has become in so many places.

When it comes to the dining outlets, they’ll include Beach Grill IK’AL (the beachfront restaurant with seafood and Yucatecan flavors), Bruma (the steakhouse), Nutre Kitchen (the all-day dining restaurant), Pool Bar Brisa (the pool bar serving drinks & light snacks), Patisserie Market & Cafe (the coffee shop), Living Room (the lobby bar).

Accommodations will range in size from 559 square feet (52 square meters) to 2,303 square feet (214 square meters), so they’re generously sized, as you’d expect. The decor looks nice enough, but not like anything special.

As you’d expect, the resort will have amenities including several pools, a full-service spa, a gym, and more.

Once open, this adds to a growing number of luxury points hotels in the Cancun area. Just recently we saw the opening of the St. Regis Kanai and Waldorf Astoria Cancun, so it’s nice to see Hyatt’s most luxurious brand also expand to the Cancun area. As a matter of fact, the Park Hyatt will be immediately next to the Waldorf Astoria (which also recently became all-inclusive, as it wasn’t initially).

The Park Hyatt brand is really growing in Mexico right now. We’ve seen the recent opening of the Park Hyatt Los Cabos at Cabo Del Sol, while the Park Hyatt Mexico City is expected to open in early 2027. Beyond that, we also saw the recent opening of the Alila Mayakoba, another good luxury option in the Cancun area.

With the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya now bookable, what are rates like? If paying cash, rooms seem to generally start at around $1,500 per night, but that does include taxes & fees. So it’s obviously very expensive, but given Mexico’s high taxes & fees, it’s actually not quite as crazy as some may have expected.

Then again, I’m not necessarily expecting this to be typical Park Hyatt quality, given the extent to which this is outside the typical Park Hyatt wheelhouse. Oddly, at least as of now, rates seem to be the same whether one or two people are staying, which is unusual for an all-inclusive.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

When redeeming points, the hotel follows World of Hyatt’s Category F all-inclusive award chart, which is the most expensive award pricing for all-inclusive properties.

Under Hyatt’s current award chart, the cost is typically 45,000 to 85,000 points per night, and that’s the same whether the room has single or double occupancy.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. The hotel is expected to be an all-inclusive, making it the first Park Hyatt property in the world where that’s the case.

It’s awesome to see Hyatt’s luxury expansion in Mexico, as this will be the third Park Hyatt to open in a fairly short time period. However, the Park Hyatt brand is becoming increasingly inconsistent, and I find the all-inclusive pivot to be a bit strange, especially given how many all-inclusive brands Hyatt already has.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya?

#6134. Ali Velshi is on the Big Board now

Six years ago, Donald Trump dropped â11th Hourâ host Ali Velshiâs name at several campaign rallies as an example of the so-called âfake news mediaâ getting what the president thought he deserved: a taste of âlaw and order.â

In May 2020, while covering the Minneapolis protests that arose in response to the murder of George Floyd, MSNBCâs live coverage caught Velshi being struck in the knee by one of the rubber bullets police fired into the crowd.

Months later, Trump referred to the incident multiple times on the campaign trail as âthe most beautiful thing,â earning laughter and applause from supporters. But an emotional Velshi recalled that moment differently in June 2026, as he said goodbye to his old weekend showâs audience.

In that moment and others, he told âVelshiâ viewers that democracy, fairness, transparency and accountability took yet another hit. âThis is how it unfolds. Not always with legislation, not always with imprisonment. Sometimes with a rubber bullet. Sometimes with a police escort. Philosophy repeated until enough people believe it. . . and they believe that the next step becomes possible,â he said. âThe press is not the enemy of the people. The press is the peopleâs guarantee that they will know what is done in their name.â

Then, he reminded everyone watching that the midterm elections were 148 days away.

When I spoke with him last Thursday, the veteran journalist repeated his belief in the pressâ witnessing role, unshaken by the massive changes occurring in the news industry.Â  One of those changes places him at the networkâs famous Big Board as the chief data reporter for MS NOWâformerly MSNBCâcarrying on an election-night tradition made famous by Steve Kornacki.

Velshiâs on-air analysis will be augmented by an additional feed called VelshiCast, a behind-the-scenes look that will stream on MS NOWâs YouTube channel.

Other aspects of MS NOWâs live coverage remain familiar to longtime MSNBC viewers, with Rachel Maddow leading the channelâs supergroup of Nicolle Wallace, Chris Hayes, Jen Psaki, Lawrence OâDonnell, Stephanie Ruhle, Michael Steele, Symone Sanders Townsend, Ari Melber and Peter Alexander.

As for Kornacki, he became NBC Newsâ chief data analyst after NBCUniversalâs owner, Comcast, spun off MS NOW along with USA Network, Syfy, E!, and its other cable channels into a venture known as Versant.

Journalism is in a precarious time, but this administration has placed particular pressure on TV newsrooms. With Paramount Skydanceâs acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, CNNâs and CBSâ teams are facing rounds of buyouts and return-to-office orders to thin their ranks. Meanwhile, Status reported that October 2026 is Fox Newsâ lowest-rated month since December 2023, with the network averaging 1.1 million total-day viewers.

Velshi remains optimistic about his profession, as he said in our wide-ranging conversation about his plans to make the Big Board even more essential on this midterm election night.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Salon: A lot of coverage cited what you said in your farewell message for your last weekend show. One of them, and I think this is important, is that you were reminding people that the show was ending 148 days before the midterm elections.

Well, weâre here now. Youâve started your weekday show, and Iâm curious to hear your impressions of how you think things are going, in terms of that dialogue with viewers and whatâs coming up about Tuesday from a data perspective.

Thanks for actually thinking that through because there is a real through line. I miss my old show a lot, but you know, that moment was so important. What I was trying to do that night, and what Iâve been trying to do since, is convey the idea that this isnât about partisan politics. This is about civic engagement. This is about democracy, and nobodyâs going to do that for you, right? Democracy is not something you pick off a shelf. It is work for all of us all the time, and I donât think weâll ever be free of a moment when democracy is on autopilot.

And so, right now, everybodyâs responsibility is to participate actively. I have a sense that pretty much all of our regular viewers, certainly people in our MS NOW community, are heavily engaged. Theyâre big consumers of news and information. They probably already voted. If not, theyâre planning to, because some people just like voting on election day because itâs exciting. But this moment wants more of us. It needs us not just to vote, but to be engaged in the dialogue, to commit to democracy, to help other people vote, to feel like we are in community with each other, to save democracy.

This doesnât matter whether youâre a Democrat or Republican or an independent, or you donât even think politics matters to you. And I will say that since that day that I left the show, Iâve only felt stronger about this, and Iâve only felt that people are understanding their assignment very, very well. And weâre seeing this from a data perspective.

Every single day, we get new data that shows early voting and advance voting. It is remarkable. At the low end, the states are up 20% compared to the last midterm elections in 2022. Weâre not even bothering to compare it to a presidential election because theyâre different beasts. In some states, early voting is up 40%. Now, what would possibly explain that? Itâs enthusiasm amongst voters. So people are going out and theyâre taking the assignment very, very seriously. Iâm very heartened by that.

So letâs talk about your new role and what you do with the data, and the conversation you have with people about that. Because I think that especially around elections, some of our pessimism and optimism comes from polling, but not necessarily from data.

Youâre 100% right. Thank you for that question too. I led the show on Monday night with three people: Kabir Khanna, whoâs our head of data and analytics; Dave Wasserman from the Cook Political Report; and Larry Sabato from the University of Virginiaâs Crystal Ball. These are the three data nerdiest guys around.

I think itâs important to understand that raw data is of no use to anyone. Even slightly interpreted data is of no use to anyone. You have to be able to look at it holistically. You have to look at polls and also understand their margins of error. You have to understand trends in polling so that even if a poll is good, meaning itâs statistically sound, that doesnât mean itâs correct. Polls have errors, and then the decision about how an election goes depends in part on polling, in part on trends, in part on the weather, in part on the news cycle, in part on whether your decision in an election is because youâre voting in favor of someone youâre excited about or youâre voting against someone youâre mad at.

I think raw data without analysis should be a crime â¦ OK, in this world where people make crimes out of everything, Iâm not sure thatâs the right thing to say. But my point is, itâs really bad. Itâs bad for democracy to throw raw data at people and hope that they interpret it. Itâs also bad for democracy to throw raw data at people and hope they follow it. Like, what am I trying to tell you? If I tell you these races are all ahead, I may not be giving you useful information for you.

So part of it is also managing expectations amongst voters. A âblue waveâ or a âbig blue wave,â I donât use that terminology . . .Â  But Iâll give you a range. Iâll tell you that as of today, the Democrats are likely to win a minimum of eight seats in the House and a maximum of probably in the mid-30s. Thatâs probably the range. Might I be wrong? Absolutely. But thatâs what I want people to understand. And then Iâm going to give you the clues to understand how I got there, so that you can follow along with me. Iâd rather make a data interpreter out of everybody who watches us than be their data interpreter.

â[P]eople are understanding their assignment very, very well.â

In terms of the election night and you being at the BigÂ  â are you guys still calling it the Big Board?

We are. Yes. I tried to call it The Magic Board of Wisdom, but no one took to that.

What you and Kornacki were doing at the Big Board really became a thing over the last decade or so.

People learned to consume election night coverage based around it. I know a lot of folks who may not necessarily watch every single moment of coverage, but keep an eye on developments with the sound off, based on whatâs going on with the Big Board. Itâs kind of like a lot of folks might go into a restaurant or a bar with the TV tuned to a game, but on mute. Iâd like to know how you feel about that mode of consumption.

Well, look: The bottom line is, scientifically, peopleâs visual consumption is their No. 1 source of information consumption. I mean, you can make the argument that smell is actually more important for your survival, but weâre not talking about survival here. The visual component hits before the auditory component does, so thatâs never going to change.

What may change is whether people watch it on their phone or their TV or, you know, through AI glasses, but the visual component is still stronger for everyone than anything else. So we spend a lot of time adjusting the size of the boxes on TV and deciding whether there are too many of them, and whether this is helpful information or confusing information. We want to make it very obvious that this is complicated information, and weâre working hard because itâs our job to present this to you in a way that is consumable and accessible. Which, by the way, has been sort of my stock in trade for my entire career.

So Iâm committed to making this the most visually easy experience. If you donât have audio, and if youâre sitting in a bar or sitting on a plane or wherever, and you canât hear me, youâll still understand everything thatâs going on.

In this election, thereâs emotional sentiment, psychological underpinnings, and consumer sentiment to account for. How much are you able to go into those factors on election night? Because each is also locally dependent. We have a lot of reporting determining the key races, but if you look down the ballot beyond the candidates, you have initiatives and other legislation driven by sentiment.

So we have two ways of measuring sentiment. One is in what we call our voter poll. Thatâs what you would know of as an exit poll, right? We do that in partnership with others. Itâs probably 1000 questions that really allow you to put meat on the bones of the result you just saw.

And I actually think thatâs one of the sad things about fast-moving election coverage, is that you sometimes donât get to sit there and say, âLet me explain to you. We actually know. We asked these voters why they made the decision they made, and they actually told us. So we donât have to extrapolate. We donât have to, you know, twist ourselves into pretzels. We actually have that information.â

âOur capabilities are better today than they were a year ago.â

So I will tell you, a lot of that will happen prior to polls closing. So people think to themselves, âYour coverage always starts before the polls close, or before the polls close in the place that I care aboutâ â thatâs actually where you get the most context. So weâre going to start early in the evening on Tuesday with our exit polls. I think we release them at 5 oâclock, and thatâs great information.

And then subsequently, we are covering every one of those ballot measures. In fact, thatâs part of what Iâm studying today. Iâm studying both the exit polls and the ballot measures today to really understand how theyâre going to correlate with the results.

You know, Iâm an economics reporter, so things like consumer sentiment are really, really clear to me. You know, people keep saying the economy is the most important thing in this election. I remind people the economy is the most important thing in pretty much every single election there is, with the exception of an actual war in which Americans have troops on the ground or an international threat. Thatâs the truth. People care most about how this affects them.

I think thereâs an interesting intersection in this election between people who care about the things that affect them, like the economy, gas, things like that, and people who care about democracy deeply. The second one can be a bit of an extra abstraction for people. The first oneâs absolutely not. So I have to measure how I tell those stories.

So Iâm going to take a little bit of a 30,000-foot view here and look at this in terms of MS NOWâs position in the news industry. On one side, you have Fox, part of a massive media conglomerate, with ratings declining right now, days before the election.

And on the other, CNN. Thereâs a lot of restructuring going on there related to the Skydance merger, a lot of conversation about that. And then thereâs you guys. Iâm wondering if, at this point, things feel different, just in terms of what youâre able to do.Â  I donât necessarily mean just kind of financial resources, but also what kind of backing Versant is giving you this time versus when you were part of the larger NBC Universal structure.Â  I realize this is still a very new situation, but again â Iâm curious about the pros and cons.

At the moment, itâs all pros. So first of all, weâre the scrappy, leaner player in the game now. . . Can we compete with other people? Yes, we can, and weâre doing it very well. As I said, the things that matter â the ability to conduct the analysis, and I donât mean that just for the big board â weâre able to do that. We are going to match everybodyâs expertise and probably exceed it.Â  Our capabilities are better today than they were a year ago.

No. 2, weâre literally the tip of the spear for the conversation that is happening in America right now around what country do we want to be. How is this solvable? Weâre right there.

And Iâm sorry for the folks around us who are dealing with these structural issues and trying to figure out what they are and how to represent themselves in this moment of turmoil, but weâre not struggling with this at all.

But we are not one thing, right? We are covering the story with all the complexity of an electorate that is spread out along the political spectrum. Iâm sure there are some of our viewers who love the idea that the [Democratic Socialists of America] is ascendant, and there are some of our viewers who love the fact that there are ex-conservatives, ex-Republicans like David Jolly running for governor in Florida. Or that there are some Republicans who are running for office because theyâve demonstrated their ability to be independent thinkers. We have the ability at MS NOW to have those discussions across the political spectrum. Weâre very comfortable with it.

In 2024, I interviewed Lawrence OâDonnell right before the election, and we talked a lot about the state of journalism, and specifically how effective the media was in terms of questioning Trump and holding him accountable. I think weâve seen shifts since then, but Iâd love to know whether youâve seen any shift one way or another.

I think so. Once in a while, maybe even daily, Iâll see some headline from a mainstream news organization that makes me cringe. That makes me think: Are these reporters and editors not understanding the moment that weâre in? Are they not understanding that that weirdly neutral headline that you just wrote doesnât actually communicate what just happened? It doesnât capture the fact that your reader and your viewer and your listener are shocked and possibly outraged and really struggling with whatâs going on. But you just wrote a headline that looks like this is just a governmental development, something that the Department of Justice did.

I think most of us are better at this than we were in 2024, and certainly better than we were in 2020 and 2016. Yes, weâve all gotten a lot better. There are still remnants in mainstream media of journalists who treat the activities of this government and this administration as normal, and thatâs not a journalistically difficult thing to unwind, right? Itâs not.

Itâs not difficult to say that journalism exists for two reasons: to bear witness for those of our consumers who cannot bear witness on their own because they canât travel to go see the scene, they canât go to the protest and they canât go to the press conference. We are there to bear witness, and we are there to hold power to account. Thatâs it. If you are not doing those two things every single day, you are not doing your job.

And there are still some members of the mainstream media who are not doing their job. This has nothing to do with what your opinion is or where you are in the political spectrum. Are you bearing witness and are you holding power to account? I think we are generally better at that. Now, what that has done is result in lawsuits. It has resulted in bans for some of us from the White House. Thatâs the consequence of doing your job properly, and thatâs okay. We will meet and face the consequences. Weâll fight back, and we will fight for our right and our viewersâ and our listenersâ and our readersâ rights to get the information that they deserve. Thatâs how you can tell weâre doing a better job at this. When they come for you, it means youâre doing your job.

MS Nowâs live election coverage begin at 6 p.m. ET/ 3 p.m. PT on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

The next time you use Clear to get through airport security, it might be faster than you've come to expect.

Over the course of this year, Clear has been expanding its new “e-gates” to dozens of airports across the country.

It's a more streamlined setup that allows passengers to fly through without stopping at one of its famous blue kiosks.

As of this week, Clear had deployed its new automated gates to 53 airports across the country.

By the end of the year, the tech is expected to be in place at nearly all the airports where the company offers its flagship Clear Plus service.

That's certainly good news for travelers looking to speed through Transportation Security Administration checkpoints — especially as the busy holiday travel rush looms.

In the past, travelers hoping to use Clear at TSA would walk up to the checkpoint, then peel off to get their identity verified with a quick photo. Then, a Clear staffer would escort them to the front of the TSA line.

While it's obviously a shortcut, the service hasn't been without pain points.

Sometimes, flyers would arrive to find no open kiosks, or have to wait for Clear staffers to be free to assist them.

The new e-gate setup is intended to improve the flow of passengers.

I've used the Clear e-gates at a handful of airports this year, and am typically able to walk through pretty seamlessly — often pausing for just a few seconds to get my photo taken before the gates open.

The company touts identity verification in five seconds or less under the new design (but do let us know in the comments what your experience was like).

As of this week, Clear had installed e-gates at nearly 80% of the airports it serves — and noted the "vast majority" of its network would have the e-gates by the end of this year.

At those hubs, the company said 96% passengers were getting through in five minutes or less.

These improvements should make the service an even better shortcut at more airports.

Clear is a paid service that lets passengers effectively skip the TSA line and jump right to carry-on baggage screening. It’s typically maximized in tandem with TSA PreCheck access.

Clear’s flagship airport security service (known as Clear Plus) now costs $219 for an annual membership.

But some travel cards will offset the cost. For instance, I get a statement credit of up to $219 each year for my Clear+ membership fee by carrying the American Express Platinum Card®, which has an annual fee of $895 (see ). Enrollment required; subject to auto-renewal.

Plus, three major U.S. airlines partner with Clear to offer special pricing: Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Alaska Airlines.

TPG Tip: If you want to try Clear and sign up using TPG's special offer, you can save $40 on the first year's membership.

Even as Clear expands its e-gates at TSA checkpoints, the program has also gotten some friendly competition from the TSA's newest security shortcut called TSA PreCheck Touchless ID.

That service, which allows members to pass through security without pulling out their ID or boarding pass, is now available at dozens of airports across the country. TSA Touchless has no extra cost for PreCheck (and Global Entry) members, though you have to opt in via your airline profile.

For rates and fees of the Amex Platinum, click .

#6131. Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways Sale: Save Up To 50% On Award Flights

Alaska Atmos Rewards offers the Global Getaways promotion, whereby members can save on award tickets in select regions. Atmos Rewards launches this promotion on the first Wednesday of each month (which the program calls “Atmos Members Day”), so we just saw the one for November launched.

Let’s go over the opportunities, as you can save up to 50% on award tickets. There are some cool markets in which you can save miles, though unfortunately only economy travel qualifies.

For the new Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways promotion, you can save up to 50% on award travel to nine destinations, with the following restrictions:

The theme for this Global Getaways promotion is “lights, camera, departure,” with the idea being to “roll out the red carpet for the destinations that have starred in your favorite films and shows.” With this sale, you can save on one-way redemptions to the following destinations (these savings are up to 50%, but not always that high):

I very much appreciate Alaska Atmos Rewards’ creativity with this promotion, as nowadays it’s pretty rare to see programs offer award sales that are also valid for travel on partner airlines. Now, admittedly I wish there weren’t quite as many restrictions in terms of the booking window, travel period, the class of service limitations, and the one-way discount, but still, there will be value here for some, and it’s better than nothing.

If you’re simply looking for the lowest cost award, some of these award prices are very tough to beat. For example, getting from the mainland to Hawaii for 11,500 points is a great deal, as is getting from the United States to India for 30,000 points. Keep in mind that with Atmos Rewards, award flights even earn status points, so could help you qualify for status.

I do hope that over time we see some first and business class award sales as well (it’s probably not happening, but we can dream, right?). Many of us have historically loved the program for the value it offers for premium cabin travel, so this promotion doesn’t help us much with that.

This is basically Alaska’s version of Air France-KLM Flying Blue Promo Rewards or Singapore KrisFlyer Spontaneous Escapes, except it applies for travel on partner airlines (rather than just for travel on the program’s airline), and is exclusive to economy (while the other promotions are mixed).

Alaska Atmos Rewards has launched its latest Global Getaways promotion, which is a monthly redemption deal offering up to a 50% discount on awards. This time around, you can save points on economy redemptions to select destinations. You need to book by November 7, 2026, mostly for travel in early 2027. While this won’t be useful for everyone, I imagine some people will get value from this.

#6129. Amex Gold Card Review: Benefits & Points For Those Who Like To Eat

The American Express® Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

The Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse if you spend a lot on food, whether it’s at restaurants or supermarkets (or a combination of both). While the card has a somewhat steep annual fee, the good news is that it offers credits that can largely help offset it. We’re also currently seeing an exceptional welcome offer, making it the ideal time to pick up this card. Anyway, enough of an intro, let’s get into my in-depth Amex Gold Card review.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

Before I get into my full Amex Gold Card review, let me summarize some of the most important features:

Here are my thoughts on the major pros and cons of the Amex Gold Card:

For someone looking to earn Membership Rewards points, the Amex Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there. To start, let’s take a look at the welcome offer on the card, along with the eligibility requirements and fees. After all, these are important factors people consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $8,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard credit pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each. So if you are eligible for a bonus of 100,000 points, those are worth $1,700, by my valuation.

This is a huge bonus, and on top of that, you have a full six months to complete the minimum spending requirement, which should be easy enough for many people to accomplish, as that translates to roughly $1,333 per month in required spending. Personally I’d only apply for the card if I got a welcome offer of at least 60,000 points (or ideally 80,000 points), but everyone has to decide for themselves what they’re willing to “settle” for.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Gold Card isn’t available to those who have or have had the card, or those who have had the Premier Rewards Gold Card in the past. Furthermore, those who have or have had an American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) may also not be eligible for the welcome offer on the card.

However, if you have had one of these cards before, you’re still eligible for the card, but you’re just not eligible for the welcome offer (which is “once in a lifetime”). In some circumstances, it could still be worth getting the card in those situations, if you’d benefit from it on an ongoing basis.

Let me emphasize that you’ll want to apply for the Amex Gold before you apply for the Amex Platinum. That’s because if you have the Amex Gold, you’re still eligible for the Amex Platinum offer, while the inverse isn’t true.

See this post for all the rules on applying for Amex cards, and see this post for details on getting approved for the Amex Gold Card.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee. There is no annual fee for up to five additional cards. Meanwhile, the annual fee for six or more additional cards is $35 for each card (Rates & Fees).

Note that Amex Gold Card authorized users don’t receive some of the same benefits as the primary cardmember, but their spending does count toward the rewards that the primary cardmember earns.

The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally. That’s especially useful when you consider that you can earn 4x points on dining abroad, all with no foreign transaction fees.

What makes the Amex Gold Card so valuable is the bonus categories it offers, in the form of Membership Rewards points. The bonus categories include the following:

This is an outstanding return on spending. Based on my valuation of Amex points at 1.7 cents each, that’s like an 8.5% return on eligible prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights.

Now let’s take a closer look at just how those bonus categories are defined.

The Amex Gold Card offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

With the Amex Gold Card you’ll earn 4x points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year at restaurants worldwide, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar spent.

Generally speaking, restaurants are defined pretty broadly, and the category includes everything from fast food to cafes to fine dining. This even includes delivery and takeout, given the popularity of that nowadays.

Just note that convenience stores, nightclubs, and restaurants located within other establishments won’t typically qualify for bonus points. Furthermore, eligibility for bonus points is determined based on how the merchant chooses to be categorized. There’s a chance that some merchants may not be categorized as a restaurant, even though you might consider them a restaurant.

For dining, this card even beats the 3x points that the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) offer — this is one of the best rewards cards for dining purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 4x points on the first $25,000 spent every calendar year at U.S. supermarkets, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar. This excludes superstores and warehouse clubs, so don’t expect you’ll be able to earn those bonus points at Sam’s Club, for example. This is one of the best rewards cards for grocery store purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 3x points on airfare, with no limits on how many bonus points you can earn. This only applies when booking directly with an airline, through the Amex Travel App™ or through amextravel.com. Furthermore, charter flights and private jet flights are excluded.

Officially, booking through online travel agencies (except Amex Travel) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice, it may still sometimes code for 3x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them. This is one of the best rewards cards for airfare purchases.

The Amex Gold Card also offers 2x points on prepaid car rentals and cruises booked through Amex Travel. This bonus category doesn’t make or break the card, but it’s a nice extra, especially if you already make these bookings occasionally.

The Amex Gold Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to about 20 partners, consisting primarily of airline loyalty programs, but also of some hotel loyalty programs.

The reason this represents such a good deal is that you can get outsized value toward first and business class travel. These tickets are often disproportionately expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal on points. On top of that, Amex often has transfer bonuses, which can stretch your points even further.

While you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than 1.0 cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

In general, I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Gold Card offers a variety of benefits that can help offset the annual fee of the card. In particular, the Amex Gold offers statement credits for eligible purchases, which could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee. Let’s take a closer look at how these work (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

The first perk is that the Amex Gold Card offers a dining credit of up to $120 per year. There are some restrictions to be aware of with this credit:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:

This is a fantastic benefit and should be worth face value for anyone who uses Uber at least once a month. Even if you don’t use Uber, this can be useful for getting food delivery through Uber Eats.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:

One thing I’d mention is that anecdotally this also works for Dunkin’ reloads, so you can always get the Dunkin’ app, and then load $7 onto your account each month, and that should trigger the credit. That’s a great way to use this to “bank” credit with Dunkin’ toward a future purchase.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards. Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year — just note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection. Benefits include a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade, if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum Card.

Holding the Amex Gold Card entitles you to a complimentary upgrade to Hertz Five Star status (enrollment required). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals. If you already rent cars through Hertz, this is a nice extra. It’s one of the more recently added benefits on the Amex Gold Card, too, since it was introduced in celebration of the card’s 60th anniversary.

The Amex Gold Card comes with a handful of travel insurance benefits that can protect your trip when you pay with your card. Check the card’s benefits guide for exact exclusions and limits, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. The Amex Gold Card is a great card for anyone who spends a lot of money on food (whether at restaurants or supermarkets), and who is looking to earn Membership Rewards points. Furthermore, the card potentially offers over $400 in annual credits, between the dining credit, Resy credit, Dunkin’ credit, and Uber Cash.

I’d argue that if you value earning Membership Rewards points, if you spend a lot on dining, and if you can use a decent number of the card’s credits, then picking up this card is a slam dunk. It’s hard to beat this kind of return on dining and supermarket spending, and it’s a great complement to some other Amex cards.

The great welcome offer that’s available is the icing on the cake, and makes applying for the card all the more tempting. I’d recommend confirming you’re eligible for a welcome bonus on the higher end of the spectrum with the current offer of as high as 100,000 points, especially because you can only get an Amex Gold Card welcome bonus once.

I will say, the Amex Gold Card might not be for you if you don’t spend a lot on dining, if you don’t live in a major city where you can easily use the credits, if you value airport lounge access as a card perk, or if you’d rather earn cash back than travel rewards, since those are all potential considerations with the card.

It’s also worth comparing the Amex Gold Card to other options. Here’s how the Amex Gold Card stacks up against some of the most popular alternatives.

The Amex Platinum Card (learn more) has a higher annual fee than the Amex Gold and comes with many more perks and annual credits. Here are the biggest differences to know about:

If you travel many times a year and want as many benefits as possible, the Amex Platinum Card is hard to beat. That said, the Amex Gold Card still offers a better return on spending when it comes to dining out and shopping at U.S. supermarkets. As I see it, the cards serve different purposes — one is about the perks, and the other is about the return on spending.

If you’re looking for a rewards card with a lower annual fee, the Chase Sapphire Preferred Card (learn more) is worth comparing against the Amex Gold Card as well. It has a much lower annual fee of $95 and fewer perks, but it still earns very strong rewards:

Between the Amex Gold Card and the Chase Sapphire Preferred, the best option for you could come down to whether you prefer Amex Membership Rewards points or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Make sure to compare your welcome bonus offers between both cards before making a final decision as well.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) is another great rewards card with useful bonus categories at the $95 annual fee level:

If you want just one rewards card in your wallet, the Citi Strata Premier makes a strong case for itself with its bonus categories. I value both Amex points and Citi ThankYou points at 1.7 cents apiece, but some travelers might prefer one rewards program over the other depending on their favorite airline and hotel partners.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is one of my favorite cards for those looking for a simple strategy, and who don’t want to focus on a bunch of credits, maximizing bonus categories, etc.

The card has a $95 annual fee, and offers a minimum of 2x miles per dollar spent, making this one of the best cards for everyday spending. The reasonable annual fee plus the flat 2x miles is ideal for someone who doesn’t maybe spend a huge amount in categories that are otherwise eligible for bonus points.

The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points. With 4x points on dining and supermarkets, earning Membership Rewards points is easy.

The card also offers some credits that are potentially useful, which for many will help offset the annual fee. The card offers up to $120 dining credits, up to $120 in Uber Cash annually, up to $100 in Resy credits annually, and up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually — a total of $424 in annual credits if you take advantage of all of them. If you don’t yet have the card, it’s seriously worth considering.

#6128. Durbin Is Retiring, Marshall Just Lost—Why The Bill Threatening Your Credit Card Rewards Isn’t Dead

Dick Durbin is retiring and Roger Marshall just lost his Senate seat. The two most prominent champions of the Credit Card Competition Act, the law intended to regulate credit card interchange which will mean far fewer rewards for consumers, will be gone in January. The bill threatening the economics of card rewards, and the airlines that depend on them, has support from President Trump and Vice President JD Vance was an original co-sponsor so it may come back with his presidential campaign. But the thing about this legislation is that it’s more useful as a way to raise campaign money from both retailers and banks than as something Congress actually passes. Departures of Durbin and Marshall haven’t made the Durbin-Marshall bill go away. Durbin identified Vermont Senator Peter Welch as his successor on the issue. The Airline Lobby Is Right To Worry In this week’s Airlines Confidential, Airlines for America CEO Chris Sununu warns that state initiatives interfering with card fees would eliminate points-funded travel. Banks buy miles because rewards help attract customers and their spending. By reducing margins on that spending, it’s less valuable to spend to encourage consumers to use the product. In markets where government has gotten involved in interchange rates we’ve seen: smaller initial bonuses higher annual fees annual caps on awards award chart devaluations (if each mile is worth less, an airline can still award one mile per dollar on spend despite receiving less money for it from the bank) It also means less revenue for the airline. In the third quarter, American Express represented all of Delta’s profit. American Airlines is barely breaking even even with several billion net from Citibank. We’d have much shakier airlines and fewer flights, and aspirational leisure destinations like Hawaii in particular would see less air service. What The Credit Card Competition Act Actually Does The current Senate bill, S. 3623, would require covered issuers with more than $100 billion in assets to enable at least two unaffiliated payment networks. At least one would have to be outside of Visa and Mastercard. Merchants get to choose the routing. That’s meant to put downward pressure on merchant payment costs by changing who controls which network handles the transaction. Cards issued in a three-party system, such as American Express issuing its own cards, are exempt from the routing requirement. Merchants benefit from accepting cards. They get more sales, and higher average sales. It’s often less expensive to accept credit cards than to take cash (due to employee theft, incorrect change, higher insurance costs). Retailers want the service cards offer, but want the government to force Visa and Mastercard to provide it for less. Trump’s promise of $1,200 in annual family savings was completely made up and inconsistent with the bill. Currently a majority of interchange gets rebated to the customer. Regulation of interchange has never lowered prices to consumers. And card payments, funded in large part by interchange, provide services to consumers beyond just payments (and borrowings). They often fund consumer protections – not just stronger dispute resolution than debit cards, but also extended warranty, return protection, and travel protections. The Bill’s Strongest Value Is As A Threat Back in July 2023, I argued that this was an especially useful issue for opening contribution wallets on both sides. Retailers have a large, concentrated interest in lowering their acceptance costs. Banks, payment networks and airlines have a large, concentrated interest in preserving the existing economics. An unresolved legislative threat gives both sides a reason to pour dollars into campaigns and political committees. I’d still bet on another round of proposals, threatened amendments and lobbying. Durbin and Marshall are leaving but the retailers and banks with billions at stake aren’t. Politicians still want the money. #6126. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as âThe most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.â

âWhen you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,â Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to âblow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.â

âIf the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,â Trump said midway in his speech. âNow that doesnât happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesnât win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.â

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report âThe party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.â The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting âthat Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.â If a sweep happens in the toss up races, itâll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.Â

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6125. Defiant Ritz-Carlton Singapore Joining Marriott Bonvoy… Finally!

The world’s only Ritz-Carlton that doesn’t participate in the Marriott Bonvoy program will finally be joining, which seems long overdue. I can’t imagine the hotel will be particularly generous, but we’ll see!

The 608-key Ritz-Carlton Millenia Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program as of December 1, 2026. So as of that date, Bonvoy members will be able to earn and redeem points, and take advantage of Bonvoy elite perks, when staying at the hotel (admittedly Bonvoy elite perks at Ritz-Carlton properties are fairly limited, as breakfast isn’t a benefit for any elite tier).

As I covered in late 2025, this property is the only Ritz-Carlton in the world that doesn’t participate in the Bonvoy program. The backstory here is that the hotel opened back in 1996, and at the time, Ritz-Carlton didn’t have any sort of a loyalty program that awarded points.

In 2010, the Ritz-Carlton Rewards program started awarding points for hotel stays, as a parallel program to Marriott Rewards. The ability to earn and redeem points came at a cost to individual hotels, but it was intended to boost occupancy and average daily rates.

Initially, hotels had the option of whether they wanted to opt in or out of the program. Most hotels bought into the concept, though the Ritz-Carlton Osaka and Ritz-Carlton Singapore were the two hotels that opted out. The Ritz-Carlton Osaka eventually decided to participate, leaving the Ritz-Carlton Singapore as the only hotel that’s not participating.

Ultimately when the Marriott Bonvoy program formed as the combination of Marriott Rewards and Starwood Preferred Guest, the hotel could still stick to its legacy contract of not having to participate in the program. Clearly the owners of the hotel have now had a change of heart… or something!

Obviously we don’t have any sort of an official explanation for the reason that this Ritz-Carlton property is finally backtracking. I can’t imagine that Marriott gave the owners an ultimatum, given that Marriott is known for letting hotel owners get away with anything, as long as they get paid.

My guess is that the competitive realities just finally caught up with this hotel — Singapore is an increasingly competitive hotel market, this is a massive hotel with 600+ rooms to fill every night, and the hotel is also a bit past its prime.

The truth is that loyalty programs exist for a reason, as they’re a great tool for getting heads into beds. Obviously the hotel will be on the hook for some additional loyalty fees, but I imagine this will make the hotel more appealing to people who otherwise wouldn’t have considered it.

I also have to imagine that even though the hotel did a decent job communicating its lack of participation in Marriott Bonvoy, I still suspect many guests didn’t realize this, and ended up being disappointed.

As of December 1, 2026, the Ritz-Carlton Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program. This is the only Ritz-Carlton hotel in the world that hasn’t participated in Bonvoy, so this is great to see.

The backstory is that the hotel opened before Ritz-Carlton had a loyalty program, and then when a program was finally formed, participation was optional. Literally every other Ritz-Carlton in the world saw value in this… except this one, apparently.

Fortunately they’ve now come to their senses, or something, so it’s great to see that this will be changing.

What do you make of the Ritz-Carlton Singapore joining Bonvoy?

I stayed in this hotel years ago and it was run like a Ritz Carlton. It was easy to be confused by their lack of participation since it is bookable via the Marriott website and they did not do a good job to discuss their non-participation. It was not just about the ability to earn and redeem points but also a lack of bonus for a Marriott hotel transaction on a co-branded credit card, at least at that time. Agree with the other comments about disliking their service but valuing their lounge.

I generally dislike this hotel and its staff, although it has a good club lounge (infinitely better than the disgraceful self-service cubby hole that the Four Seasons Singapore calls a club lounge.) The hotel is gargantuan, impersonal, and noisy. The hotel's location is poor, and nothing is walkable (not that Singapore is particularly walkable with its heat and pollution at particular times of the year). After 20 years of annual travel to Singapore, I would still greatly prefer any number of hotels in Bangkok or Hong Kong. I am tired of the "we will read from our luxury script and you will be delighted" style of service in Singapore, where the customer is always wrong for wanting something personal or customized that is not an option on the script. Same thing on SQ.

About time. That said, beyond accumulating and using points, benefits are few and far between at Ritz Carlton properties to begin with. But hey, at least you can earn and use points now. For what it's worth, this is a nice, though somewhat dated property. The location is good, the views are great; note there is noise from the expressway even on the 40th floor if you're facing NE .

The Ritz in London, Paris and, under Mandarin Oriental in Madrid, have no affiliation with Bonvoy. The only original Ritz-Carlton hotels in North America are in Montreal and Boston with the latter now the Newbury. The modern ones, under Marriott, seem lesser to me. There are other choices.
