#6055. Democrats better hope they don’t have another Manchin in their midst

Ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk. The whole country has seemed to be in a sour mood, unhappy with everything, feeling as if the world has gone off its axis and life is out of balance. The trauma of that experience was probably far deeper and more injurious than we wanted to admit, so we just sort of sleepwalked as events cascaded around us, feeling emotionally distanced and impotent.

We finally woke up and shook it off. For the first time in six years, the American people took back control of their own destiny and issued a stunning, overwhelming rebuke to the Republican Party, which had fallen back into power during that period of national somnolence and took a wrecking ball, figuratively and literally, to the country. America, it seems, decided to save itself.

The historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated. Analysts assured us that while it looked likely the party would gain at least a House majority, the so-called real victory would be if Democrats reduced the margins in red states, which would serve as a warning to Republicans that they had gone too far. Nobody really expected that Democrats would actually win in places like South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa or perhaps even Mississippi, where, as I write this, Democrat Scott Colom has a 43-vote lead over GOP incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Political polarization was assumed to be set in stone; the GOP’s redistricting gambit and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act meant that Democrats could not expect to flip more than a handful of seats, and the party was facing one of the most inauspicious midterm Senate maps in recent memory. At this moment, they are expected to end up with 245 to 255 seats in the House and possibly 55 seats in the Senate, an unthinkable outcome as recently as yesterday morning.

It will be a while before we see the final tally, but the results are so obviously decisive that even Donald Trump cannot fatuously claim that this election was stolen. All the threats against election workers and plans to contest the outcome are empty in the face of such a victory. It is finally, once and for all, clear that the country does not want the insanity and chaos that Trump has wrought.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

According to voter polls — formerly known as exit polls — the top issue for voters was the cost of living, as expected. Reversing the tariffs and putting an end to the war with Iran would be the obvious ways to begin to alleviate some of the stress, followed by restoration of funding for healthcare and other vital safety net programs. Rolling back Trump’s tax cuts for the wealthy would go a long way as well. But the president Trump has already promised to be “Mr. Veto,” so the prospect for a new era of bipartisan comity with the White House does not look good.

It’s always possible that congressional Republicans will feel chastised enough that they will work with Democrats to create veto-proof majorities on those issues, but I wouldn’t hold my breath. The best the Democrats can hope for is that Trump decides he needs to do something positive for his legacy besides building his ballroom and renaming the Atlantic Ocean, and he agrees to compromise on something. I wouldn’t hold my breath on that either. But that doesn’t mean Democrats shouldn’t pass the legislation — and make Trump and Republicans block it.

Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

As great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that big tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Roosevelt’s long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the New Deal agenda.

Eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently it’s always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginia’s Joe Manchin and Arizona’s Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.

In the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives “overreading the mandate,” the reality is that everyone else understands that the most important priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this issue there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll showed that 90% of voters said that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say that’s a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.

Whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

#6048. House GOP races to lock down new leadership after blue wave

A sweeping tide of Democratic wins Tuesday left Republicans preparing for a new face atop the House GOP leadership ranks as the party gears up to defend President Donald Trump from a list of investigations.

It’s shaping up to be a battle between sitting Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, pitting two lawmakers Trump has publicly praised against one another.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana had been trying to stay the course before Republicans dropped a stunning amount of seats, including ones considered deep-red. The cascade of losses, which will give Democrats a sizable majority in the 435-member chamber, forced Johnson to stand down. He told his staff on a Wednesday morning call he would not seek the minority leader job for the next Congress when the GOP conference votes behind closed doors next week.

In a possible sign of what’s to come when the often-raucous conference meets to hear from candidates and vote, some GOP insiders were split Wednesday on which lawmaker should take over as leader.

“It might be Jordan’s for the taking. I think the real fight will be at whip and conference chair,” said one GOP source with ties to each member’s office, granted anonymity to be candid.

In a letter to colleagues Jordan circulated Wednesday, he pitched himself as “battle-tested on the oversight front,” which could help as Democrats go full-tilt on probing the Trump administration. “For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democrat majority,” Jordan’s letter reads.

But another person familiar with Scalise’s thinking said “his No. 1 goal will be to lead the conference back into the majority,” describing Scalise as a “proven and tested leader who is ready on day one.”

“The conference knows him, how he fights, and that he’s a trusted leader,” the person said.

Spokespersons for Scalise and Johnson did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment on their plans.

Heading into the midterms, it appeared Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the sitting majority whip, had been working behind the scenes to shore up his standing with House GOP members in a bid to become the No. 2 Republican in January.

Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger of Texas has also pitched himself for minority whip, writing in a Wednesday letter to colleagues that he believed his conference needed “fresh ideas” and had “missed many opportunities.”

The scope of Tuesday’s losses had some calling for a completely clean slate, with Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., posting a message on social media to House and Senate brass: “Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction.”

“Having Jordan and Emmer in as leadership won’t be much of a change at the top,” the first GOP source said. “But President Trump should want a warrior like Jordan with impeachment experience in charge, given the Democrats will inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

To that end, Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, likely the incoming House Judiciary Committee chairman, said in a brief interview before the chamber adjourned in September to campaign that “there’s a long list of potentially impeachable offenses” to look at from the president, his family members and inner circle.

An aggressive investigatory push by Democrats could make Jordan, in Trump’s eyes, an attractive candidate to lead the conference. Jordan fought hard against Trump’s two first-term impeachments, including with fiery cable news hits that were praised by the TV-focused chief executive.

Whatever happens, it will cap off a rocky ride for Johnson, who claimed the gavel in the tumultuous weeks after Kevin McCarthy was ousted as speaker in October 2023.

In a statement released early Wednesday morning, Johnson did not reveal his next move.

“While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning. This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history,” Johnson said. “However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world.”

Notably, during a phone interview with Politico late Tuesday night, Trump was asked about Johnson — but did not endorse him for minority leader.

“I think he’s done a very good job,” the president said, his voice hoarse from an October-long rally blitz that did not pay off for his party. “I mean, they’re going to have to make that decision. He’s going to have to make that decision. But he’s a good person and a good man.”

On Wednesday Trump told reporters at the White House he intended to stay out of the coming House GOP leadership race.

While Republicans are eager to avoid repeating the bitter public battles of the past, the fight for minority leader is in some ways a rerun. Both Scalise and Jordan tried for the speaker’s gavel back in 2023 after McCarthy’s sacking but neither landed the job.

A former high school and college wrestler who later coached grappling, Jordan was once considered too much of a firebrand to lead the entire caucus.

“Early on he wasn’t really given the opportunity to show what he’s capable of because of his steadfast conservative positions,” Ray Yonkura, who was Jordan’s chief of staff for a decade and has done political work for him, told CQ Roll Call in October 2023. “He was oftentimes pushed to the side, or different Republican leaders tried to keep him down.”

“Once he was given an opportunity to show what he’s capable of, I think a lot of people realized that this is somebody whose skill set can actually be good in a leadership role,” Yonkura said then.

Jordan has faced questions over the years about what he knew about sexual abuse by a doctor at The Ohio State University when he worked there as an assistant wrestling coach starting in the 1980s. He has repeatedly denied knowing of the abuse, and multiple Republicans told CQ Roll Call in 2023 that it hadn’t factored into their support for Jordan.

As for Scalise, he went through a public ordeal in 2017 when he was shot by a gunman at a GOP baseball practice, sustaining serious injuries. He later was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, and in 2024 said he was in remission.

Beyond the House leadership shuffle ahead of the start of the 120th Congress, G. William Hoagland, a former Senate GOP leadership aide, said there would be a broader battle among Republicans as they analyze their losses and look ahead to 2028.

“I take Steve Bannon’s comment recently seriously that the Republican Party will be engulfed in a civil war over the future of the party,” he said, referring to recent comments from Trump’s former chief 2016 campaign and White House strategist. “Expect that civil war to play out over the next couple of weeks in the midst of all the other legislative issues they have to deal with in the lame-duck session.”

Niels Lesniewski, Savannah Behrmann, Paul Krawczak and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

“The issue is not me,” Schumer told reporters outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Wednesday morning when asked about working with those new senators. “The issue is focusing on the American people and what they want.”

The leadership election for Senate Democrats will likely take place in early December and include the senators-elect in a secret ballot race.

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who won a Senate election against Republican Michele Tafoya, told NBC’s Meet the Press NOW in August, “I think it is time for new leadership,” when asked if she’d support Schumer.

She reupped that sentiment on a Wednesday press call, saying, “Many of us were elected who refused corporate PAC money, who are beholden only to the people who elected us, and are ready to fight for bold change. And so I think it’s time for new leadership.”

Schumer has served in both the minority and majority as Democratic leader after landing the job in 2017 when then-leader Harry Reid retired. He faces reelection in 2028.

Former state Senate President Troy Jackson of Maine, the Democrat who defeated Republican Sen. Susan Collins in her bid for a sixth term, told reporters on Monday, “I’ve already said that I told Sen. Schumer that I’m gonna support somebody else. It’s no different now.”

He said he would push Schumer to deliver on health care changes like “Medicare for All.”

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, who bested John Sununu in his bid to return to the Senate, said in an interview last week that “it’s very clear voters are hungry for new voices at the table and for a new generation of leadership in the Senate.”

“I’ve heard that throughout this campaign. I think above all, people want folks who understand the challenges out there and are going to fight with the urgency that these challenges deserve,” he said. “Too often, we’ve seen leadership flat-footed.”

His campaign did not immediately respond to questions Wednesday about whether that was indicative of his support for Schumer.

Democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist church who unseated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, told CNN in September: “I’m not supporting Schumer for leader.”

“I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer, but we need new leadership. We need new, younger leadership, young blood. I don’t mean just age, but people who are bringing fresh ideas and fresh leadership,” he said. “We’ve got to have leaders that can unite us, bring us together. Not just Democrats, but bring together Democrats and Republicans to solve real problems.”

“I think people are frustrated with the gridlock and the sense that people are not working together,” he added, pointing to Democrats blocking the farm bill in the Senate Agriculture Committee earlier this year.

Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan, told MS NOW earlier this fall he would want to support Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen as leader.

“I would definitely support Sen. Chris Van Hollen and I would love to see him as Senate majority leader,” he said.

Van Hollen is seen as a presidential contender, and has been “kicking the tires” on 2028 instead of Senate leadership when he’s been asked.

El-Sayed told NBC’s Today Show on Wednesday, just hours after his race was called, “We need action. We need leadership toward that action. I’m interested to see, working with our caucus, to see what options we’ve got,” saying he hopes there is “two or more options” but not mentioning Van Hollen.

“I’m going to vote for the option that gives me the best chance at getting money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All,” he said.

Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton made it part of her Senate primary pitch earlier this year that she was the only Democrat in the race who didn’t support Schumer. “I’ve made it clear that I would not support Chuck Schumer as leader of the Democratic caucus because I think right now what I’m hearing from voters all across the state of Illinois is that they are fed up. They’re fed up with what’s happening in Washington,” she told political YouTube commentator Jack Cocchiarella in March.

A spokesperson for Stratton’s campaign reiterated Wednesday her position hasn’t changed. The campaigns of El-Sayed, Hamilton and Jackson did not immediately respond to questions Wednesday about their stances.

Even if some candidates were eager to distance themselves from establishment Democrats on the campaign trail before facing voters, it’s hard to deny that Schumer helped bring home a resounding victory for Democrats on Tuesday night.

So far, among Democratic incumbents, it’s not clear anyone would have the appetite to challenge Schumer, who flexed his political prowess and recruited several of the key flips last night, like former and incoming Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio to recapture the state for Democrats.

Having prevailed in a special election, Brown is expected to be seated before the end of the year.

A Democratic staffer familiar with the current mood of the caucus predicted: “Nope. Schumer will be the leader,” when asked if there was any serious challenger.

Former Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota had a similar prediction. “Given the big night Senate Democrats had, I doubt anyone will challenge him. But some new members may withhold their vote, in keeping with their campaign comments,” Daschle said.

Schumer on Wednesday said Democrats will be united in addressing costs for the American people with what he described as “an amazing crop of new senators” and a “generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America not only now, but on into the future.”

“These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want. They entrusted us with the majority to do what they, the American people, want,” he said. “Republicans received that opportunity two years ago and completely squandered it. The GOP misread Americans’ demand for change as a mandate to do Trump’s self-serving bidding, and Trump spent half his time talking about things that were irrelevant to their lives.”

#6041. A New USAID Can Be Smarter and Sharper

Argument: A New USAID Can Be Smarter and Sharper

“A very good morning,” I said in Spanish, smiling at the young director of the Colombian National Land Agency as we exchanged congratulatory handshakes. It was 2024, and my U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) team and I had just arrived to inaugurate new offices for the land agency in downtown Bogotá, where fresh staff and IT systems would help speed the laborious and typically yearslong process of turning paperwork into official land titles.

It had taken years of hard work and millions of dollars of aid to bring reform to Colombia’s dysfunctional land administration system, in which more than 40 percent of rural landowners lacked proper titles. Over several years, we had carefully researched ownership in several key counties, and now it was the land agency’s turn to convert our surveys into official titles.

“A very good morning,” I said in Spanish, smiling at the young director of the Colombian National Land Agency as we exchanged congratulatory handshakes. It was 2024, and my U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) team and I had just arrived to inaugurate new offices for the land agency in downtown Bogotá, where fresh staff and IT systems would help speed the laborious and typically yearslong process of turning paperwork into official land titles.

It had taken years of hard work and millions of dollars of aid to bring reform to Colombia’s dysfunctional land administration system, in which more than 40 percent of rural landowners lacked proper titles. Over several years, we had carefully researched ownership in several key counties, and now it was the land agency’s turn to convert our surveys into official titles.

Looking at the elaborate setup, I turned to my program manager and asked under my breath, “How much did we pay for this?” USAID contractors always footed the bill for such events, in my experience. “Nothing,” he replied. “This is their show.”

This memory epitomized for me both the promise and dysfunction of my 21 years at USAID. We existed to bring such transformational reform to life, within the governments of our host countries. Yet we were hampered by our own systems and practices.

The end of USAID’s operations in September 2025 was a tragedy—for U.S. soft power and influence, for the lives in developing countries that have been lost, and for the shameful treatment of USAID’s foreign and American staff. But the agency was not perfect, and as we look toward building back something better, we need to think sharply about how to make a system more interested in transformation than paper-clip counting.

I recognized much of what frustrated me with USAID in the pages of Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s 2025 bestseller, Abundance—too much paperwork, pursuing low-risk and low-impact approaches when we knew better ones, and stymied by process over outcomes.

USAID generally spent its funding through competitively awarded grants and contracts to NGOs and for-profit contractors. These entities would, in turn, hire experts, rent out offices, and buy vehicles and equipment to provide expertise to the host-country organization.

In this case, our contractor was a big, for-profit U.S. firm. Staffed by very capable Colombians, it was always a struggle to get our contractors to see why the real goal was for the local government to take over. The contract required deliverables, such as 20,000 land titles issued, not the deeper reforms that the inauguration of the new offices represented.

The whole system of measurement and incentives within USAID worked against these moments. Our standard indicators counted units, such as the number of people trained, but had no way to measure transformation. The auditors were notorious for only finding fault and lack of compliance, not handing out kudos. Nothing in any of our systems awarded us for the host country, rather than ourselves, taking on responsibility for a project.

These are not entirely new questions. In former USAID Administrator Andrew Natsios’s widely read 2010 essay, “The Clash of the Counter-Bureaucracy and Development,” he detailed how USAID had become consumed by compliance and paperwork, spending “as much money on oversight and control as on implementation.” Worse, it had strayed from its mission of creating transformational partnerships with developing countries in favor of low-risk, countable outputs.

I moved to Washington in 2000 and worked as a management consultant for federal agencies until 2004, when I became a foreign service officer with USAID. The practices and acronyms Natsios described were our bread and butter—inspector general audits, performance measurement, and strategic planning. I naturally carried that skillset over when I began my USAID career. My last tour was as deputy director in Colombia, the largest USAID program in the Western Hemisphere. As I became a senior USAID officer, Natsios’s critique rang truer and truer to me.

A perennial directive during my 21 years at USAID was to push us, working in the field missions, to work more with local partners. Most recently, the goal of former Administrator Samantha Power’s localization initiative was to provide 25 percent of USAID’s total funding in direct contracts and grants to local partners. The Biden administration ended with still a long way to go to meet that goal, reaching only 12 percent of funding.

The development theory was simple; partners more involved in designing and managing programs would produce more sustainable programs that they saw as their own, not as the donor’s. To be sure, done poorly, there were plenty of potential downsides to giving direct grants to local partners, such as heightened corruption, aid dependency, and exacerbating local power dynamics as local elites would often control this funding.

But there were other potential advantages, too. Locals tend to understand how to get things done in their own country and may devise more appropriate solutions, and grants to local partners often cost less to implement.

Despite all these efforts, most of our funding went to grants to large international NGOs, the United Nations, or to big contracts with for-profit firms that had developed around implementing specialized USAID funding, known as “Beltway bandits.” Most USAID staff instinctively knew that local partners would have a better angle on problems. But we also knew that it was just too complicated and time-consuming to do it at scale.

Natsios described the situation in 2010 as one where the complexity of working with USAID, “restricted newer, smaller, and local organizations from competing for grants and contracts, because these organizations lack the business systems to follow U.S. federal law and regulation, to account properly for all funds, to disburse money quickly, and to produce measurable and auditable results.”

In 2025, 15 years after Natsios published his essay, the situation was about the same or perhaps marginally better with regard to the proportion of USAID funding globally going to local organizations, probably increasing by a couple of percentage points, from 10 to 12 percent.

In Colombia, the proportion going to local organizations was far less than the global average—only about 5 percent of our funding went to local partners. The rest went to large international NGOs, the U.N., and Beltway bandits. Speaking as someone partly responsible for this situation, this was insane.

Colombia, while having significant development challenges and needs, is considered by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development to be an upper-middle-income country. It has a highly developed private sector and state. The challenges noted by Natsios of “lack of business systems” were much less an issue in a place such as Colombia, yet we provided very little of our funding to local partners. Our complicated design and contracting processes were the same whether the grant was $100,000 or $10 million, disincentivizing smaller projects—while USAID’s complexity put off local partners. We had clear incentives to spend but no penalties for not working with locals. And we had the staff to manage 20 large grants but not 100 small ones.

When I ask myself how we could move from the bureaucratic, risk-averse, and process-focused USAID to a new and redesigned foreign assistance that is bold and transformative, my answers stem from my own experience—and the limited number of projects I felt were truly successful. In my 21-year career, I probably worked on or led just five or six projects I would consider to be absolutely transformative out of dozens of projects. Other work was good, but it did not have the same feeling of real change.

I felt that difference powerfully one night in Kabul in 2016. We were running a virtual online auction at the U.S. Embassy, where private sector investors from around the world would bid on a new 10-megawatt solar farm project in Kandahar. The CEO of the Afghan utility and his senior staff accompanied us in person, and we watched on a TV monitor as bids came in from companies. The numbers slowly got better and better as the night progressed. When bidding closed, the Afghan government had a deal at a world-class price from the winning company.

This moment meant that the Afghan government could negotiate with the global private sector, equal to equal, without donors as intermediaries. The teary-eyed CEO hugged me and immediately called the Afghan president to tell him the good news.

No standard indicator can capture that moment, and it was not featured as a headline in the next audit report. Yet that moment was so transformative that this approach to infrastructure was repeated to great effect by the Afghans on their own. The Afghan government used the private investor approach we piloted with them that night to triple the output of Kajaki Dam with Turkish investors over the next few years.

Models exist within USAID and federal foreign assistance to pull from. Down the hall from me in Bogotá sat the lead for USAID’s Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) program. I was envious of the fact that she wasn’t there that often but instead out in the field working directly with communities on small infrastructure or community projects. OTI’s model was completely different than the rest of USAID. Field managers were expected to be in the field, bonding with counterparts, adjusting programs, and making things happen. Back-office contract and finance work was done in Washington. If I wanted to get a read on the political dynamics at a key counterpart agency, my first stop was to speak to the OTI rep.

The Inter-American Foundation (IAF), a much smaller U.S. federal body, also worked with those small communities and NGOs doing truly grassroots development work. In Colombia, it worked with small Indigenous-led NGOs serving their community or women’s groups helping them to start small businesses—organizations often without offices or full-time staff.

How did IAF do it? Its procedures were completely different from ours, its funding scale was generally under $100,000, and it included a key condition in making these grants. It generally requested that an NGO’s own contribution be at least as much as IAF’s, ensuring that this was the NGO’s project and the NGO owned it.

Global problems are landing on U.S. shores in unprecedented numbers. The right focuses on migration and illegal drugs, while the left sees climate change and pandemics. However you weigh each of these threats, they could all be mitigated by well-designed foreign assistance.

I know this is the case because I managed such programs in Colombia just prior to the mission’s closure. We helped Venezuelan migrants take advantage of generous policies that would allow them to stay in Colombia, rather than start their hike to the United States through the Darién Gap. Other programs incentivized coca farmers to stop growing coca and make their livelihood legally. Climate finance preserved hundreds of thousands of acres of virgin forest to slow climate change. Funding helped Colombia’s health ministry prepare for the next pandemic. Foreign assistance is not a panacea but remains an essential tool to protect the United States.

As Natsios reminds us, development is about building institutions “in poor and fragile states, with the ultimate goal of developing a capable state, market economy, and civil society.” It’s not about bean-counting. It is time to think boldly about how we could redesign foreign assistance around that objective and help solve the threats facing the United States.

Jeremiah A. Carew was the deputy mission director of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) in Colombia from 2021 until the mission’s closing in August 2025. Over his 21-year career with USAID, he served in Peru, Afghanistan, Uganda, Vietnam, South Sudan, and Washington, D.C. He retired at the rank of counselor in the U.S. Senior Foreign Service, and his final assignment was as mission director of USAID in Somalia. He currently resides in Ecuador, where he writes on international development topics for Razón Pública in a monthly column; his work has also appeared in El Tiempo and the Foreign Service Journal.

#6037. Washington Is Debating the Wrong AI Risk

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Washington Is Debating the Wrong AI Risk

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Washington is gripped by an artificial intelligence (AI) panic, driven by the prospect of superintelligent models delivering our doom. Today’s Nostradamuses include whistleblowers from frontier AI companies—who put the odds of AI killing all humans at greater than one in 10 and warn that insiders expect it could happen before the end of the decade—and anti-nuclear activists, who note that it wouldn’t be the first time humanity built something that could kill us all. The doomsayers may yet be right, but their scenario rests on a long chain of assumptions, each highly unlikely on its own and far less likely to align all at once.

This doesn’t mean AI isn’t dangerous. But by fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios, we miss the forest for the trees: the common, mundane AI dangers already present and actively causing harm. The pressing AI risk Washington should focus on more is automation bias, the phenomenon where humans over-rely on or over-delegate to AI relative to the accuracy of AI models, off-loading cognition to the machine, sometimes even in the face of contradictory evidence.

Washington is gripped by an artificial intelligence (AI) panic, driven by the prospect of superintelligent models delivering our doom. Today’s Nostradamuses include whistleblowers from frontier AI companies—who put the odds of AI killing all humans at greater than one in 10 and warn that insiders expect it could happen before the end of the decade—and anti-nuclear activists, who note that it wouldn’t be the first time humanity built something that could kill us all. The doomsayers may yet be right, but their scenario rests on a long chain of assumptions, each highly unlikely on its own and far less likely to align all at once.

This doesn’t mean AI isn’t dangerous. But by fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios, we miss the forest for the trees: the common, mundane AI dangers already present and actively causing harm. The pressing AI risk Washington should focus on more is automation bias, the phenomenon where humans over-rely on or over-delegate to AI relative to the accuracy of AI models, off-loading cognition to the machine, sometimes even in the face of contradictory evidence.

The high-profile insistence on AI safety to address the risk of extinction from AI superweapons created by the most advanced large language models (LLMs) distracts attention from the urgent risks we should and can begin to solve now: human errors in operational usage of AI today due to automation bias.

A Chinese-flagged container ship transits the Gulf of Oman on Oct. 13. AFP via Getty Images

This spring, during the U.S. war with Iran, it appears that an intelligence report suggested that China was sending nuclear weapons components on a ship in the Middle East toward Iran. The U.S. military immediately began surveillance and made plans to intercept and board the vessel. Just before the operation began, officials reexamined the original report. They discovered it came from an analyst who forwarded an AI model’s output that stitched together intelligence to suggest the ship carried nuclear components. The report was false, with the AI model either incorrectly identifying or hallucinating the nature of the vessel’s cargo.

It’s easy to blame the AI for the false report. But what matters more is that the analyst didn’t check what the model had generated, and neither did the planners who received the report. The analyst entered the fabricated AI claim into a standard intelligence report that went up the chain of command, and no one checked until it was almost too late. Better AI or guardrails on AI models would not have solved the problem.

For those who know their Cold War history, this should ring alarm bells. In September 1983, Soviet early-warning satellites reported that the United States had launched nuclear missiles. The duty officer, Stanislav Petrov, judged it a false alarm and declined to report it up the chain as an attack. He was right, and he likely averted nuclear war. This spring’s episode was, in essence, a Petrov incident without a Petrov. In 1983, a machine raised a false alarm and a human had the presence of mind to question it. This time, a machine raised a false alarm, and the human analyst passed it along. The error surfaced only on a last-minute second look.

It’s evident to anyone how close of a call this was, and how near to danger we came. Sen. Mark Warner recently stated that for Congress to take real action, we will need a “holy heck moment.” This near-miss incident probably won’t qualify—it drew a fraction of the attention and news coverage given to this summer’s Hugging Face incident, in which OpenAI models escaped their testing environment and breached the company’s servers—but it should. The episode did not go unnoticed, on the other hand, in China, where one news outlet described the failure as one wherein the machine “merely handed over a crooked ruler,” but humans were the ones who ultimately did the measuring.

Talk of “super intelligence” distracts from frequent screwups.

Beijing has a strategy. Washington has a voluntary pledge and a “Super Intelligence Force.”

Just as British people did with steam power, the American public can shape how this technology spreads.

The near-miss regarding the Chinese ship is not the only example. Airline pilots fall prey to automation bias when they ignore their instruments and training and trust the autopilot too much, causing tragic plane crashes that have killed hundreds over the past three decades. Automation bias in drivers occurs when navigation software routes them onto a closed road (as in the famous Allstate commercial); instead of using their eyes and judgment, they follow it anyway. For the military, a classic example happened in 2003, when Patriot missile systems in Iraq classified friendly aircraft as incoming missiles, and operators approved engagements that killed British and American troops.

Despite its prevalence today, this type of human error does not feature heavily in the AI argument now consuming Washington. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for slowing frontier development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman warns that humanity could lose control of AI, while U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed the push for restrictions as a “conspiracy.” The current debate focuses on guardrails for what labs build and the potential for doomsday scenarios. One explanation for the focus on doomsday scenarios is that      they capture the public imagination. Another is that they distract from the complicated reasons that real-world accidents often occur. Accidents regularly result from the interactions among people, organizations, and technologies. The tendency in the non-AI accident realm (think a plane crash) is to blame the pilot, rather than the complex system and interaction among the pilot, their training, and the technology that leads to the accident. We could be seeing the AI version of that dynamic, where the AI becomes the scapegoat.

But the near-miss with the Chinese ship shows what can happen if we continue to ignore the risks with AI systems that already exist and are already being (mis)used.

In January, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released an Artificial Intelligence Acceleration Strategy designed to put AI tools in the hands of 3 million military and civilian personnel at every classification level. Scaling AI adoption is essential to U.S. military power, but it must happen responsibly to be effective. The new strategy emphasizes expanding access to data, compute, and AI tools from warfighting to intelligence to enterprise, and even special hiring authorities for AI talent. The next step, conspicuously missing from the AI Acceleration Strategy, is training to ensure commanders and operators understand the advantages and risks of the AI systems they use.

Automation bias is not inevitable, and if the American government, including but not limited to the military, can address it, the United States can lead the world in AI adoption with responsible speed. Based on our experience working in the Pentagon and doing research on practical AI risks, two changes would help the United States capture the benefits of AI and mitigate much of the risk.

U.S. Army cadets take notes during a lecture on terrorism at the United States Military Academy in West Point, New York, on March 30, 2007. Don Emmert/AFP via Getty Images

First, create standard operating procedures for managing AI outputs. For example, any finished intelligence product that used a generative AI tool should say so, visibly, to everyone who reads it. The analyst in this recent incident reportedly used AI to both query intelligence reports and then to package the findings, and in this final report failed to disclose AI use, making the report’s content look human-generated. Furthermore, AI inferences in intelligence reports should require confirmation beyond the AI model for high-risk decisions. Boarding a Chinese vessel during an ongoing war would have been incredibly risky. Speed that leads to operational failure isn’t useful. One additional operational check can make a huge difference without substantially slowing things down. This does not only apply to intelligence products, though there is a unique risk there—but also to any output aided by AI tools, including in the use of AI decision-support systems.

The second is training. In co-authored research, we found that people with the least experience with AI models were the most likely to defer to them, a version of the Dunning-Kruger effect applied to machines. Familiarity built through structured training, including exposure to these systems failing, produces better, more effective AI users. In more recent work, we found that West Point cadets exhibited automation bias in 3.9 percent of trials, compared with 9 percent in a matched sample of the American public, suggesting that military education can help produce personnel who interrogate algorithmic outputs to maximize their effective usage instead of merely accepting them.

The danger of automation bias will not be engineered away by better models or models that never hallucinate, because the failure comes from how people use them. The military is not helpless here. Solving AI risk is more about people and organizations than engineering, and it’s not an imagined problem for tomorrow.

Michael C. Horowitz is the director of Perry World House and the Richard Perry professor at the University of Pennsylvania, and a senior fellow for technology and innovation at the Council on Foreign Relations. X: @mchorowitz

Lauren Kahn is a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

#6036. How redrawn House districts voted in the midterms

House Republicans were banking on their  redistricting power play as a firewall against Democratic gains. Tuesday’s blue “tsunami” tore right through it.

Redraws of congressional maps across the country reshaped the fight for the House, putting new districts on the battleground and setting up some surprisingly close races. But as of early Thursday, Democrats appeared poised to lose only a few gerrymandered seats, and potentially none held by a Democrat seeking reelection.

In North Carolina and Tennessee, both states where Republicans redrew the maps, GOP incumbents whose seats had been considered safe or on the periphery of the House battleground were trailing as of Wednesday.

“We made it clear last year … that Republicans might start this redistricting and gerrymandering. Democrats were going to finish it. And last night that’s exactly what happened,” Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat, said at a news conference Wednesday.

President Donald Trump kicked off the redistricting effort last summer, when he called for Texas to redraw its congressional lines. Democrats responded in California, where voters approved a new map that would give the party five pickup opportunities.

In total, nine states held elections in 2026 under new House maps, and attempts to redraw the congressional lines in other states fell short. Virginia Democrats were dealt a setback when the commonwealth’s Supreme Court invalidated a Democrat-led redraw that voters had approved via a referendum. Similarly, the U.S. Supreme Court blocked Republicans from using a redrawn map in Missouri, which voters rejected via a referendum Tuesday.

Efforts to adopt new maps in Republican-led Indiana, South Carolina and Georgia also came up short.

Here’s how candidates running in redrawn districts fared on election night:

As of Wednesday evening Democrats had held four of the five seats that Texas Republicans targeted through redistricting.

32nd District: Republican Air Force veteran Jace Yarbrough narrowly defeated Democrat Dan Barrios, a former Richardson City Council member, in a redrawn district that would have backed the president by 18 points in 2024.

9th District: The Houston-area district would have backed Trump by 20 points under the new lines, but Democrat Leticia Gutierrez comfortably held the seat for her party over Republican Army veteran Alex Mealer.

35th District: Democrat Johnny Garcia, a former Bexar County sheriff’s deputy, defeated Republican Air Force veteran Carlos De La Cruz in a redrawn San Antonio-area district that Trump would have carried by 10 points.

28th District: Longtime Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar’s South Texas seat was another Republican target, but he defeated party-switching Webb County Judge Tano Tijerina in a landslide.

34th District: Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez coasted to reelection over Republican Eric Flores, a former federal prosecutor, in a redrawn Trump +10 South Texas district.

Texas Democrats also flipped the massive 23rd District, which hugs the U.S.-Mexico border and the 15th District in South Texas.

Florida Republicans were hoping to pick up as many as four seats under their new map, but Democrats have held on to at least three of them.

9th District: Rep. Darren Soto, who went into Election Day as the most vulnerable House Democrat, was clinging to a narrow lead over Republican Navy veteran Dan Green in a redrawn Central Florida seat that Trump would have carried it by 18 points.

14th District: Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor held off a challenge from Republican former state Rep. Mike Beltran, despite her Tampa Bay district transforming into one that would have backed Trump by 11 points.

22nd District: Democrat Pia Dandiya kept this open South Florida seat in party hands, defeating Republican Casey Askar in a Trump +10 district.

25th District: Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz defeated Republican former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer in a Trump +9 district that hosted one of the most expensive House races this year.

Ohio was required under state law to draw a new map ahead of the 2026 elections. In a surprise, Republicans and Democrats on the state’s redistricting commission struck a deal that resulted in new lines that favored the GOP, but not as much as Democrats had feared.

9th District: Rep. Marcy Kaptur, the longest-serving woman in congressional history, won her rematch against Republican former state Rep. Derek Merrin by an even wider margin in a Toledo-area district that would have backed Trump by 11 points.

1st District: Rep. Greg Landsman had no trouble winning reelection over Republican Eric Conroy, a former Air Force intelligence officer, in a redrawn Trump +3 district in the Cincinnati area.

In addition, Ohio Democrats had flipped the GOP-held 7th and 15th districts as of Wednesday afternoon.

It wasn’t a surprise that North Carolina joined the GOP-led redistricting push; the new 2026 map was the state’s six in seven election cycles and gave Republicans the edge in 11 out of 14 seats. The primary focus of the new GOP-drawn map was the 1st District, but shockingly, as of Wednesday afternoon, six Republican incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chair Richard Hudson, were trailing in their reelection bids.

1st District: Rep. Don Davis’ Eastern North Carolina seat grew more competitive under the new map, shifting to one Trump would have carried by 12 points. But the second-term Democrat was leading Republican Army veteran Laurie Buckhout at publication time.

After the Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais ruling that weakened parts of the Voting Rights Act , the court allowed Alabama to use a new map that would favor Republicans in a district that had been drawn the previous cycle as a second Black-opportunity district.

2nd District: This plurality-Black, Kamala Harris-voting district was redrawn as one Trump would have carried by 14 points. Nevertheless, Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures comfortably prevailed over Republican state Rep. Rhett Marques.

After the Supreme Court invalidated Louisiana’s congressional map under the Callais ruling, state Republicans adopted new boundaries expected to help them flip one seat.

6th District: The new map eliminated the majority-Black seat created the previous cycle, which the Supreme Court ruled was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander. Democratic Rep. Cleo Fields opted to run for the state Senate instead of seeking reelection in a redrawn Trump +32 district. This year’s election reverted to Louisiana’s “jungle” primary system, with all candidates running on the same ballot. And with no one likely to take a majority of the primary vote, the top-two finishers will advance to a Dec. 12 runoff.

Tennessee Republicans moved quickly after the Callais ruling, adopting a map that gave them the advantage in all nine of the state’s House seats.

9th District: The Memphis-based district, a formerly deep-blue bastion, was dramatically redrawn as a seat Trump would have carried by 21 points. And yet Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor was barely ahead of Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson as of Wednesday afternoon.

California’s new voter-approved map led to significant reshuffling in the state delegation, setting up a member-versus-member fight and prompting Republican Rep. Kevin Kiley to become an independent.

1st District: Republican James Gallagher, who topped CQ Roll Call’s final list of the most vulnerable House members, lost to Democratic former state Senate leader Mike McGuire in a Harris +12 Northern California district. Gallagher won a June special election under the old lines to succeed the late GOP Rep. Doug LaMalfa.

3rd District: The new map redrew Kiley’s 3rd District as a solid-blue Sacramento-area seat, prompting Democratic Rep. Ami Bera to seek reelection here. Kiley opted for the slightly-less-blue 6th District but was defeated by former Democratic state Sen. Richard Pan.

22nd District: GOP Rep. David Valadao saw his purple Central Valley seat moved a tad left, though Trump would still have carried it. Still, the Republican lost to progressive Democrat Randy Villegas.

41st District: Redistricting dismantled Rep. Ken Calvert’s Riverside County seat, and he opted to challenge fellow GOP Rep. Young Kim in the deep-red 40th District. Democratic Rep. Linda T. Sánchez won the new 41st, now a blue stronghold in Los Angeles County.

48th District: Republican Rep. Darrell Issa announced his retirement after the new map transformed his deep-red Southern California seat into a purple battleground. Democrat Marni von Wilpert, a San Diego city councilmember, was leading Republican Jim Desmond, a San Diego county supervisor, as of Wednesday afternoon.

A Utah judge approved a new map that gave Democrats a pickup opportunity and set off a round of musical chairs among the state’s four Republican House members that culminated with Rep. Burgess Owens opting to retire.

1st District: Democratic former Rep. Ben McAdams defeated Gen Z Republican Riley Owen in the new district, anchored in deep-blue Salt Lake City.

Analysis: Reigniting War With Iran Would Be a ‘Huge Gamble’

Growing signs suggest that U.S. President Donald Trump could restart the war with Iran following the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.

While there have been renewed diplomatic efforts to reach a deal over the past week, the terms Iran has put on the table—including lifting all U.S. sanctions—would be difficult for the United States to accept. Meanwhile, Trump has offered mixed signals on what he plans to do, indicating that he hasn’t yet made a decision. Over the weekend, Trump said the war could be over soon, but he also said that the U.S. still had to “take care” of one or two nuclear sites and would have to give Iran “the hammer” at some point.

Growing signs suggest that U.S. President Donald Trump could restart the war with Iran following the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.

While there have been renewed diplomatic efforts to reach a deal over the past week, the terms Iran has put on the table—including lifting all U.S. sanctions—would be difficult for the United States to accept. Meanwhile, Trump has offered mixed signals on what he plans to do, indicating that he hasn’t yet made a decision. Over the weekend, Trump said the war could be over soon, but he also said that the U.S. still had to “take care” of one or two nuclear sites and would have to give Iran “the hammer” at some point.

The war has cost U.S. taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion so far and has left the United States military depleted on a number of levels—from drastically reducing key munitions stockpiles to the destruction of expensive equipment and aircraft.

The U.S. is estimated to have used up to 65 percent of its Patriot air-defense interceptors and 80 percent of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) ballistic missile interceptors since the war began, for example. The U.S. stockpile of Tomahawk cruise missiles is estimated to have fallen from around 3,000 to 2,000 since the fighting started, and the war has reportedly left its stocks of missiles for the Army Tactical Missile Systems, or ATACMS, and precision strike missiles almost exhausted. Around a quarter of the U.S. military’s MQ-9 Reaper drones have also reportedly been lost during the war. Rebuilding these stockpiles will take years.

All of this raises questions about U.S. military readiness and capabilities if Trump chooses to return to war post-election.

The United States still has significant military capabilities in the Middle East, including over 50,000 troops and two aircraft carrier strike groups. Another aircraft carrier strike group is en route and should arrive near the end of this month.

Longer-range and more advanced capabilities like Tomahawk missiles are “significantly depleted,” and Patriot and THAAD batteries are “limited,” but there are “other ways for the president to be able to successfully execute the missions he’s looking at,” Jonathan Panikoff, the senior director of the Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council, told Foreign Policy.

“In the short term, the U.S. is likely quite ready to carry out the planned operations,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a senior fellow and director of the defense program at the Center for a New American Security. An additional Patriot unit was sent from Texas to Israel, for instance, and the Pentagon has likely dispersed aircraft and personnel from bases that are very close to Iran and less well defended, such as in Bahrain and Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, Pettyjohn said.

But that’s just the short term. The picture could change drastically over a longer time horizon.

“The long-term readiness concerns are quite profound,” Pettyjohn said. These constraints include “munitions stockpiles”—for example, long-range standoff attack missiles and defensive interceptors—“deferred ship maintenance, and disrupted readiness cycles, which affect what forces will be available for future contingencies.”

The U.S. has reportedly told Gulf allies to brace for a short but intense campaign targeting Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, with the goal of strengthening Washington’s negotiation position. But Trump has consistently struggled to dictate the direction of the war, and Iran has proved to be a resilient adversary. The U.S. and Israel conducted thousands of strikes on Iran, but Tehran has not budged in its demands. Iran has also exhibited an ability to quickly adapt its tactics and has proved that even with a diminished military, it can disrupt the flow of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

“If Iran has prepared for a more protracted campaign of attacks against U.S. forces in the region and civilian infrastructure, that could quickly drain near-term U.S. readiness. So overall, restarting the war would be a huge gamble,” Pettyjohn added.

Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei during a recent meeting with commanders reportedly said that Iran’s response would be “immediate, effective” and “without any geographical limitations.” Iran would likely move to strike U.S. bases in the region and energy facilities in Arab countries in response to the war restarting, but it has also signaled that a wider menu of civilian infrastructure could be targeted.

“It is impossible to defend everywhere,” Pettyjohn said. “The U.S. can in the short term surge fighter aircraft to help interdict incoming drones and to potentially suppress Iranian launchers, although the latter must fly over Iran and is at risk of being shot down. But that is a difficult posture to sustain indefinitely as aircraft are likely operating from more distant bases, flying long sorties, and require lots of tanker support.”

Resupplying forces that are under attack with additional weapons would be difficult as well, Pettyjohn said.

The decisions that Trump makes with regard to Iran will also have an impact on U.S. military capabilities in other theaters moving forward. The “more capabilities” that are used against Iran, Panikoff said, “the less that are available for other potential conflicts in the future.”

John Haltiwanger is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @jchaltiwanger.bsky.social X: @jchaltiwanger

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the key issues in the U.S. midterm elections, cyberattacks targeting Russia and Ukraine, and Iran’s proposal to end the war.

Democrats and Republicans made their final pitch to voters on Monday in the run-up to Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. Early polling suggests that Democrats will likely win back control of the U.S. House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate in what would be a crushing blow to President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement. According to experts, the White House’s poor handling of the Iran war could be to blame.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the key issues in the U.S. midterm elections, cyberattacks targeting Russia and Ukraine, and Iran’s proposal to end the war.

Democrats and Republicans made their final pitch to voters on Monday in the run-up to Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. Early polling suggests that Democrats will likely win back control of the U.S. House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate in what would be a crushing blow to President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement. According to experts, the White House’s poor handling of the Iran war could be to blame.

In the eight months since U.S. and Israeli forces first launched strikes on Iran, fuel prices have skyrocketed, energy infrastructure has come under fire, and fighting has upended critical supply chains. Products from batteries to medical supplies to sulfur have borne the brunt of the U.S.-Iran war. And the wallets of U.S. voters are far from immune to the fallout.

The cost of living for the average American household has grown by around $2,000 since the war began, according to economists at Moody’s Analytics, or roughly $265 billion for U.S. consumers in total. Coupled with Trump’s continued tariff war with Canada, dissatisfaction with high inflation rates has dropped Trump’s approval rating to 38 percent, per NBC News’s polling average.

Democrats are capitalizing on these figures to try to win control of one or both chambers of Congress. Doing so would give them more leverage to challenge Trump’s foreign-policy agenda, such as by blocking Trump’s national security nominees, cutting off further military funding for the Iran war, investigating alleged corruption within the president’s inner circle, and even trying to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Republicans, meanwhile, tried to distance themselves from Trump’s Iran policies on Monday and instead focused on tried-and-true conservative talking points, such as the need for immigration crackdowns, low taxes, and the (unsubstantiated) threat of Muslim lawmakers in office.

Trump echoed a few of these arguments during a speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday. “We have to keep our Congress strong, free, a little bit of apple pie,” Trump said, adding, “We’re not looking to have a jihadist be in our Senate,” in a thinly veiled reference to Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is vying to represent Michigan.

Yet Trump spent the bulk of his remarks—originally advertised as a closing midterms campaign speech—discussing topsoil, graffiti stains, piping, algae, limestone, and other construction elements of his capital renovation projects.

It is unclear if these issues will be enough to convince voters to back the Republican Party.

Trump has already vowed to “veto everything” if Democrats take back Congress. In an interview with the New York Post published on Monday, the U.S. president did not rule out issuing preemptive pardons to his aides and allies, such as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company recently came under heavy criticism after the Trump administration reportedly cut off Ukraine from military-grade Starlink internet services. And the administration has already asked the U.S. Supreme Court to temporarily block around 20,000 mail-in ballots from counting in California as part of its growing bid to sow distrust in the U.S. electoral system.

Tuesday, Nov. 3: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung hosts Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni hosts Chilean President José Antonio Kast.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosts Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda.

Wednesday, Nov. 4: Israeli President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with party leaders.

Friday, Nov. 5: Chinese President Xi Jinping hosts Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.

Saturday, Nov. 6: New Zealand holds a general election.

Pope Leo XIV begins a multiday trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru

Monday, Nov. 8: Turkey begins hosting the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference.

G-7 foreign ministers hold a two-day meeting in France.

Phony alerts. Residents in Ukraine and Russia received phony emergency alerts late Sunday and early Monday that warned of high radiation levels, chemical threats, ballistic missile attacks, and on-the-ground fighting. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of hacking the Ukrainian emergency alert app and said his country had hacked Russia back in response.

The messages, some of which were riddled with spelling errors, did not appear to worry many locals. However, the cyberattacks did cast new uncertainty over the security of both nations’ emergency alert systems. It also highlighted the very real and ongoing threat of Russian ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine. On Friday, the United States unveiled a $2.1 billion deal to supply 500 more Patriot interceptors to Ukraine; however, sources told Reuters that it could take years for the missiles to arrive, even though Kyiv currently has inadequate air defenses.

This week’s incident occurred just as a limited cease-fire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky expired on Monday. U.S. first lady Melania Trump had negotiated the six-day truce to allow humanitarian aid to reach the devastated city. However, on Monday, Kyiv accused Moscow of using the pause to strengthen its military position in the area. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov responded that any troop movements there were “standard practice” and that Ukraine likely did the same thing.

Last-ditch negotiations. Iran announced a two-day plan on Monday that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the United States. The deal, which could be implemented within a week, would only occur if Washington agreed to meet Tehran’s seven conditions for ending the war. Those include an end to the U.S. military blockade on Iranian ports, a U.S. waiver on Iranian oil sales, and the cancellation of new U.S. sanctions on Tehran, among other concessions.

“The basis of dialogue ​and talks between Iran and the U.S. via mediators is still Iran’s seven-step proposal, which is now condensed, making it possible to implement it within two days,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said. Trump, however, rejected that deal in September and has since repeatedly threatened to launch fresh strikes on Iran.

“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice,” Trump said on Sunday at a campaign rally. “But at some point, we’re going to have to give them [Iran] the hammer.” Whether such a resumption of fighting will ultimately happen—and if so, when—remains anyone’s guess. Asked on Monday if he’s considering striking Iran after the U.S. midterms, Trump simply said, “No.”

Meanwhile, Persian Gulf nations are preparing themselves for a possible return to heavy fighting, which they expect could trigger Iranian retaliatory strikes on their civilian infrastructure. Alongside deadly Houthi strikes on Saudi energy facilities, experts fear that the region is not ready to absorb renewed warfare. “Gulf producers spent five decades persuading the world that their supply could withstand regional wars,” Amir Handjani wrote in Foreign Policy. “Eight months of fighting on two fronts have badly weakened that case.”

A win for Moscow? Acting Bulgarian President Iliana Yotova won the country’s presidential runoff on Sunday, making her Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state. According to the Central Election Commission on Monday, Yotova clinched 57.6 percent of the vote, putting her in double digits ahead of former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who secured 39.5 percent. She will be inaugurated on Jan. 22.

Yotova’s win marks a larger victory for the country’s ruling Progressive Bulgaria party. The Russia-friendly group, led by Prime Minister Rumen Radev, secured 131 seats during parliamentary elections in April. Yotova retaining power means that the party’s agenda will now have even less resistance, as Radev and Yotova are united in their support for lifting international sanctions on Moscow as well as their opposition to providing Ukraine with further military assistance.

At the same time, Yotova and Radev have both sought to maintain Bulgaria’s European friendships. Being a member of NATO and the European Union has forced Sofia to exercise a delicate balancing act of fostering closer relations with Russia while also not angering Bulgaria’s traditional allies. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Yotova on her win on Sunday, writing on X, “From security and defence to our competitiveness and energy independence, I look forward to continuing our joint work.”

Four continents, 30 countries, 31,000 miles. English adventurer Karl Bushby completed his 28-year journey around the world on Monday, walking from Punta Arenas, Chile, to his mother’s home in northern England. During that time, he dodged war in the Darién Gap, was airlifted to safety while crossing the Bering Strait, and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel. Visa struggles, the 2008 financial crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic came close to sapping his resources for good, but the now 57-year-old explorer remained adamant on completing his odyssey entirely on foot. “They say it takes a village, but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said.
